articles.title_orig: Donald Trump China Putin Jinping
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump China Putin Jinping
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SEOUL — President Trump will get his wish for a historic meeting among the three most powerful men in the world — Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and himself — at a summit Thursday in southern China.
But Moscow, Beijing and Washington already know their leaders are arriving at the Shenzhen conference with disparate aims.
Trump hopes to focus the meeting on nuclear nonproliferation, urging the Russian and Chinese presidents to work with him to scale back the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles. Putin pressed for the meeting to discuss his ongoing war in Ukraine . And Xi wants to discuss neither, only embracing the idea of the summit to show the world China can help broker peace on the international stage, Chinese officials told The Times.
“That’ll be interesting,” Trump said earlier this week,  teasing the trilateral summit before the White House formally confirmed the meeting Friday.
“We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he added, “but we’ll be talking a lot of things.”
U.S. officials have acknowledged they do not expect the meeting to result in a breakthrough on arms control. China is openly racing to build up its nuclear capacity — a nonnegotiable policy in Beijing, which sees its arsenal dwarfed by an American stockpile nearly 10 times the size.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement. I would characterize this as the entry point,” one senior Trump administration official said. “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
Trump’s break from long-standing tradition in U.S.-Russia relations was real, but it should not have been entirely surprising.
The Chinese, too, threw cold water on the chances of a breakthrough, with one Chinese official telling The Times the central government saw no benefit to a pause.
“It is a matter of survival,” the official said.
The United States and Russia still command the world’s two dominant nuclear arsenals, with over 5,000 warheads each. China has an estimated 620 — but in catching up, it is developing new warheads with more sophisticated delivery systems.
Moscow, too, is modernizing its weapons, after the Trump administration allowed the last major U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty to expire earlier this year.
Though expectations are low for a nuclear breakthrough, Trump doesn’t want to discuss Putin’s priorities, either, the U.S. official added.
“He does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting,” the official said. “China is not really part of that track, so it doesn’t really seem appropriate.”
Ukraine has grown increasingly concerned by Trump’s pressure campaign to force it into concessions to Moscow as he pushes to end the war.
The Trump administration has brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at a working level to explore the viability of peace talks. But a long-standing U.S. policy on the war — not to negotiate about Ukraine without Ukraine — could be further compromised at a trilateral with Putin and Xi.
The only American business leader confirmed to join Trump in Asia is Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who was seen as instrumental in the decision last month to restrict Ukraine’s access on the battlefield to Starlink , the satellite internet service owned by Musk.
Beijing has struck a careful balance on Ukraine, publicly issuing its respect for sovereign borders — a position popular among Chinese voices who support Kyiv — while giving Moscow diplomatic cover, an economic lifeline and technological support throughout the war.
The summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
Their competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that hark back to the famous Yalta Conference — held in Crimea, the Ukrainian peninsula currently occupied by Russia, in 1945 — where Josef Stalin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Winston Churchill carved up a postwar order.
The summit on Chinese soil offers Xi a powerful image to broadcast worldwide , demonstrating an emergent superpower can bring together the leaders of two historic rivals in the name of peace.
Putin gets to present himself as a global player, despite the devastation wrought on Russia’s economy and military standing after four bruising years of war.
And it allows Trump to reassert his global relevance after this month’s midterms delivered the worst electoral rebuke to a president in half a century, rivaling the backlash against President Nixon during Watergate.

articles.title_orig: COP31 Talks Collapse in Turkey in a Clash Over Fossil Fuels
articles.title_zh: COP31 Talks Collapse in Turkey in a Clash Over Fossil Fuels
articles.content_orig:
COP31 President Murat Kurum, center, leaves a closing plenary session at the U.N. Climate Summit, Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from fossil fuels like coal and natural gas. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption
ANTALYA, Turkey — International climate change talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours over the main cause of planetary warming — fossil fuels. On Sunday, nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from energy sources like coal and natural gas.
The talks ended in a dramatic fashion, with the European Union negotiators saying they could not agree to a final agreement without mentioning the transition away from fossil fuels — the primary driver of climate change. The EU bloc then walked out of the room. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal make up roughly 73% of global emissions .
After representatives of the EU walked out, other countries also objected – including Panama and island states such as the Marshall Islands.
The European climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, said that when the world is heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."
This is the first U.N. climate summit where there's been scientific consensus that the world will surpass a key global warming threshold. Countries agreed in 2015 to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.
Negotiations at this year's U.N. Climate Summit were supposed to end Friday but there was no agreement on language about fossil fuels. Activists demonstrated by holding signs that read "shame" at COP31, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption
Passing that threshold means more severe climate impacts , like more intense hurricanes and heat waves. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius would require cutting emissions immediately, reducing them by 45% by 2035 . That, scientists say, would require dramatically cutting fossil fuel use.
"It's good that that decision has been rejected," says Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, a nonprofit focused on climate change in Africa. "It doesn't have enough to help protect the people who are most vulnerable to climate change, who have contributed the least and are now suffering firsthand the worst."
NPR correspondent Michael Copley contributed to this story. This story was edited by Sadie Babits .
A previous version of this story incorrectly said the European Union walked out along with other countries. In fact, EU representatives walked out while other countries objected.

articles.title_orig: Libya's eastern government suspects drone attack caused explosion on Russian ship
articles.title_zh: Libya's eastern government suspects drone attack caused explosion on Russian ship
articles.content_orig:
Satellite imagery showed a ship on fire at the port early on Sunday morning
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.
The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.
It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.
Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.

articles.title_orig: Court bans China’s BYD from selling ‘Defender clone’ SUV in EU
articles.title_zh: Court bans China’s BYD from selling ‘Defender clone’ SUV in EU
articles.content_orig:
Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach
The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.
Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel .
The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.
But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.
“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”
Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.
Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.
“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”
The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.
The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.
“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement .
“The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.
The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.
The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.
Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited .
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia . Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

articles.title_orig: Taiwan warns Canada over dependence on China
articles.title_zh: Taiwan warns Canada over dependence on China
articles.content_orig:
U.S.-China commission leaders warn of growing Chinese military capabilities, threats to Taiwan and risks to American security ahead of Trump’s summit with Xi and Putin.
President Donald Trump faces a potentially dangerous "two versus one" negotiating scenario when he meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, two senior members of a congressional China watchdog warned Wednesday, raising concerns that Beijing could seek concessions on Taiwan while Moscow pushes for greater U.S. pressure on Ukraine.
"I think it is two versus one. We have China and China's junior partner, Russia," Randall Schriver, chairman of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told Fox News Digital in a Zoom interview. "Largely they come to the table as a team versus President Trump and the United States," he said, citing China's support for Russia's war in Ukraine.
TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES
President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as President Xi Jinping watches, before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa/Pool via Reuters)
The warning comes ahead of Thursday's planned trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China , on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The high-stakes talks are expected to address issues such as the wars in Ukraine and Iran, trade and nuclear weapons.
Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chairman, echoed Schriver's assessment, arguing that Moscow's growing dependence on Beijing puts Trump at a disadvantage.
"Putin is a client state of Xi Jinping, and that essentially means that President Trump is in the room with a two against one scenario, and the stakes are significant," Kuiken told Fox News Digital.
"China is fueling Russia's war machine in Ukraine, and they are basically the lifeblood of the Russian economy at this point," he added.
TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA
Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Sputnik/Sergei Bobylyov/Pool via Reuters)
The commissioners spoke as the bipartisan body released its 2026 annual report to Congress , detailing Beijing's expanding military, technological and economic capabilities and the growing challenges they pose to American national security.
Asked what would constitute success or failure at the summit, Kuiken suggested Beijing would not have agreed to the meeting without assurances that its interests would be protected.
"My assessment is that the Chinese would never have agreed to this meeting if they had not had significant assurances that essentially nothing would happen," Kuiken said.
Schriver warned that both Xi and Putin would seek opportunities to advance their strategic objectives. He suggested Beijing would pursue gains related to Taiwan, while Moscow would hope Trump emerged from the meeting prepared to increase pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy .
CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet at the Great Hall of the People on May 14, 2026, in Beijing, China. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
"If Putin had his way, Trump would emerge from the meeting and put more pressure on Zelenskyy," Schriver said.
He also questioned whether sufficient diplomatic groundwork had been laid for meaningful nuclear arms control discussions, one of the issues Trump has indicated he wants to address.
"President Trump would like to talk about nuclear disarmament, probably an agenda that makes sense. I'm just not sure we've done the front-end work when it comes to interagency work, bilateral or trilateral work, at a lower level to have a productive discussion there," Schriver said.
Nevertheless, Schriver suggested that avoiding concessions could itself represent a successful outcome for Washington.
"I think holding ground and just a restatement of U.S. interests is probably a victory of sorts for us," he said.
Responding to the commissioners' warnings, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington defended the trilateral meeting as an opportunity for cooperation among the three powers. "The three presidents will have an in-depth exchange of views on safeguarding world peace and enabling strategic stability in major-country relations. The summit is of groundbreaking significance," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital.
The spokesperson emphasized the three nations' shared responsibilities as permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, arguing that closer communication would serve global stability. "It is in the interest of the three countries to strengthen communication, manage differences and maintain stable relations. This is also the expectation of the international community and is conducive to global stability and dialogue and cooperation," the spokesperson said.
CHINA’S IRAN TIES COMPLICATE TRUMP-XI SUMMIT AS TENSIONS TEST US LEVERAGE
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) fabrication plant in Phoenix, Arizona, on March 3, 2025. (Rebecca Noble/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Beyond the summit, the commissioners warned that the United States faces mounting challenges as China approaches 2027, the benchmark year associated with Xi's directive for the People's Liberation Army to develop the capability to conduct a Taiwan military operation.
Asked whether Washington was doing enough to deter Chinese military action against the self-governing island, Schriver gave a blunt assessment.
"I think the short answer is no, we're not doing enough," he said.
Schriver pointed to a pause in congressional notifications for U.S. arms sales to Taiwan , saying the commission wants those notifications to proceed and supports stronger security assistance for the island.
He also warned that Beijing's increasingly sophisticated coercion tactics extend beyond conventional military operations to include actions involving its coast guard.
"We do talk about counter coercion capabilities and blending not only military capabilities but law enforcement that the Chinese are doing, this sort of blended lawfare with their coast guard east of Taiwan," Schriver said.
Taiwanese conscripts during a visit by Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te to a military base in Taichung on June 28, 2024. (Sam YehAFP via Getty Images)
"It's a tough challenge as we're entering the benchmark year that Xi Jinping said of 2027. There should be more attention to this and there should be greater efforts to this."
Kuiken emphasized Taiwan's importance to the global technology supply chain, particularly its role in manufacturing advanced semiconductors used in artificial intelligence.
"Taiwan is the island at the center of the world. Xi Jinping is obsessed with it," he said.
Pointing to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, Kuiken warned of the broader implications for American technological leadership if Beijing were to take military action against the island.
He urged Washington and its partners to develop a coordinated strategy to make an invasion or other Chinese coercive measures against Taiwan unattractive to Beijing.
President Donald Trump meets with delegations from Japan, India and Australia at the Solaire Hotel, on Nov. 17, 2026, in Manila, Philippines. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
Responding to concerns about Taiwan , a U.S. official told Fox News Digital, "There is no change to our policy with respect to Taiwan." Asked about the commissioners’ warnings, a White House official emphasized President Trump’s diplomatic approach to China and his plans to discuss nuclear arms reduction during the trilateral summit.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Is Racing to Keep Its Booming Defense Industry From Stalling
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Is Racing to Keep Its Booming Defense Industry From Stalling
articles.content_orig:
“If China were to decide to restrict its exports, Ukraine as well as the rest of Europe and the US would feel that immediately,” says Igor Nakonechnyi. The CEO of Project Foundation, a Ukrainian bid to build chip capacity in Europe, tells EU Perspectives why the drone industry depends on China and what Europe can learn from Ukraine’s frontline.
The war in Ukraine has exposed how heavily the world’s drone industry relies on China for critical components . The Fourth Law is a Ukrainian defence technology company that develops autonomous drones for use on the battlefield.
Together with its sister company Odd Systems, which supplies drone cameras, it is working to establish semiconductor manufacturing capacity in Europe through an initiative called Project Foundation. The two firms want to reduce reliance on Chinese suppliers and address a vulnerability that affects Ukraine’s drone industry and Europe’s wider security.
In the interview, Igor Nakonechnyi describes the daily struggle to source components amid sudden shortages and price hikes. He also explains why the company is opening an R&D hub in Eindhoven, why many EU funding programmes take too long to pay out, and why the Chips Act should cover dual-use technologies.
Our company was created in response to Russian aggression. Our team already had quite some experience in entrepreneurship and consumer electronics, so they were looking at how they could best use their skills in the face of the aggression.
Drones are a defining feature of modern warfare. One of the key components of a drone is a camera. Basically, they are the eyes of the drone.
The real bottleneck here is the thermal sensor — a semiconductor chip that allows a camera to detect heat. China can make around 20 million of those a year. Every thermal drone needs a sensor, so whoever controls sensors controls how many thermal drones can be built.
Outside China, it is pretty much only North America and France that have some manufacturing capacity, which is maybe a couple of million in total. That’s a huge discrepancy, and we see it as a huge vulnerability.
Indeed. If China were to decide to restrict its exports, Ukraine as well as the rest of Europe and the US would feel that immediately.
Even if we haven’t yet seen a full restriction, there’s already always a shortage of specific things, or the price suddenly goes up. — Igor Nakonechnyi, CEO of Project Foundation
Even if we haven’t yet seen a full restriction, there’s already always a shortage of specific things, or the price suddenly goes up. It’s a constant challenge that our procurement team deals with on a daily basis.
That’s a critical vulnerability that we want to solve not only for Ukraine, but also for Europe and the rest of the world. That’s exactly why we launched Project Foundation, to build thermal-sensor fabs in Europe and the US, so the West no longer depends on China for the eyes of its drones.
We are currently setting up a subsidiary in the Dutch city of Eindhoven, where Project Foundation is headquartered and will serve as one of our main R&D hubs.
We see ourselves as part of Europe. And we see a lot of opportunities and talent in Europe to build this with.
I see that a lot of relevant stakeholders already understand this, and more and more are becoming aware. In the US, even more so: more money is being invested in sovereign production, specifically of military equipment. This has always been the case, but investment is growing even more now. In Europe, it’s gradually getting better.
To be clear: my company does not receive any EU funding at the moment. But we are looking at a few funding calls.
However, we see that many funding programmes have timelines that are simply too slow for us. If you want to apply for funding, it can easily take a year before you actually get it. So you need to write a project, wait almost a year until you get the money, and then you have two or three years to build a prototype.
Even within a year, warfare in Ukraine will have changed completely, and the concept you requested funding for might no longer be relevant. — Igor Nakonechnyi
That timeframe doesn’t match modern warfare. Even within a year, warfare in Ukraine will have changed completely, and the concept you requested funding for might no longer be relevant.
There are more agile programmes coming, but we need more of them. We really need more speed.
Yes, that’s a very good initiative, but a big problem for us is that it’s primarily for civil use and not dual use. For example, what we are working towards—thermal-camera sensors or image sensors—is not really part of the Chips Act, whereas we believe it is an important topic.
We are talking about semiconductor manufacturing here, so it makes sense from that perspective. We do already see dual use in, for example, the Industrial Accelerator Act [a proposed EU law aimed at boosting manufacturing and demand for European-made and low-carbon products].
The reality of today’s world is that many different things are interlinked. Embracing dual use in, for example, the Chips Act would reflect that reality.
Our company is originally driven by demand in Ukraine, but we of course want a just and lasting peace for Ukraine. And that peace only lasts when there’s a strong, independent defence industry behind it to deter another war. We hope to continue contributing to that; not only for Ukraine but for the wider Western world.
We see ourselves as a global company, and also hope to use our products in civilian applications in the future, such as consumer robotics and cars. We don’t want this to end up only in the hands of China.

This is the first U.N. climate summit where there's been scientific consensus that the world will surpass a key global warming threshold. Countries agreed in 2015 to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.
Negotiations at this year's U.N. Climate Summit were supposed to end Friday but there was no agreement on language about fossil fuels. Activists demonstrated by holding signs that read "shame" at COP31, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption
Passing that threshold means more severe climate impacts , like more intense hurricanes and heat waves. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius would require cutting emissions immediately, reducing them by 45% by 2035 . That, scientists say, would require dramatically cutting fossil fuel use.
"It's good that that decision has been rejected," says Mohamed Adow, of Power Shift Africa, a nonprofit focused on climate change in Africa. "It doesn't have enough to help protect the people who are most vulnerable to climate change, who have contributed the least and are now suffering firsthand the worst."
NPR correspondent Michael Copley contributed to this story. This story was edited by Sadie Babits .

articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 entered correction territory after U.S. stocks fell 3.7% Friday, leaving the index more than 10% below its recent peak after it broke its 200-day moving average. Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research and one of Wall Street’s biggest bulls, said the selloff has gone too far and is a correction rather than a bear market, according to BeInCrypto.
Yardeni cited healthy corporate earnings and cheaper valuations, and still expects the S&P 500 to reach 8,500–9,000 by the end of 2027, though he sees no immediate trigger for a sharp recovery. Last year’s Liberation Day crash reversed after Trump changed course on tariffs, but investors may have to wait longer for a rebound this time. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said inflation remains a serious concern and raised the possibility of a half-point rate hike in December; markets expect further hikes in December and January. UBS strategist David Lefkowitz also expects slower growth and weaker AI spending. U.S. consumer sentiment rose roughly 7% in November to its highest level since August. Upcoming inflation data and December’s Fed decision will test whether rate hikes push the economy toward recession and undermine Yardeni’s recovery outlook.

articles.title_orig: Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the conflict began
articles.title_zh: Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the conflict began
articles.content_orig:
Reported attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the Iran war began, maritime data shows, as Tehran seeks to re-exert its control over the critical waterway amid falling oil prices.
In October, the number of attacks reported to the Royal Navy-affiliated United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) exceeded 30 for the first time since the US-Iran war began in late February.
As of Sunday, at least 22 attacks were reported in November, the second highest figure since the war began, according to a CNN analysis of UKMTO data. The reporting area covers the Strait of Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman.
Before October, the number of reported attacks in the region averaged around 10 per month. Numbers vary, but data from the International Maritime Organization also points to October as having the highest number of confirmed incidents so far this year.
Since the conflict began, the strait has become a heavily contested frontier , with attacks there disrupting oil and gas shipping and sparking global economic fallout.
Iran began trying to halt traffic in the wake of the US-Israeli attacks that launched the war. In response, the US imposed a blockade on Iranian ports, and as CNN previously reported , Gulf producers have found ways of getting ships through the strait.
Commercial traffic through the channel – through which a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war – remains at a reduced level when compared to the 2025 baseline.
As global oil prices fall and the Iran’s domestic crude revenues come under increasing strain, Tehran has been stepping up attacks, with experts saying the country is losing its leverage over the waterway and could escalate attacks further in an attempt to force concessions from Washington.
The International Energy Agency attributes the recent decline in oil prices to a recovery in Gulf exports. Prices also fell after the US midterm results as concerns over fresh US military action in the Middle East subsided.
“Markets appear to be increasingly assuming that a return to full-scale war is unlikely and that oil supplies will gradually recover,” Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank, told CNN . “But that assumption could change quickly if Iran decides to intensify the confrontation.”
Meanwhile, Iran’s domestic oil revenues are falling sharply as the US blockade of Iranian ports continues to stifle the country’s supply of oil to global markets, according to maritime data tracking service Kpler.
“Iranian oil on water outside the (US) blockade zone has hit zero as the last cargoes discharged in China earlier this month. Consequently, Iran’s oil revenues could drop to zero by mid-December,” Kpler reported in late October.
US President Donald Trump said this month the US doesn’t “need a deal” with Tehran and ordered Vice President JD Vance to turn his focus elsewhere .
“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed!” Trump posted on Truth Social. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”
He later indicated he wouldn’t hesitate to resume military strikes in Iran if necessary.
During the latest attacks, projectiles struck three tankers exiting the strait on Friday and Saturday, according to Marisks, a maritime risk management company.
Marisks did not confirm who was behind the attacks, though it said Iranian involvement was “assessed as likely.”
Trump says Iran is ‘bullsh*tting’ on effort to end war
Fire erupted aboard the Captain Leon, a Marshall Islands-flagged chemical and oil tanker, after it was struck at the bow at 3 p.m. UTC (10 a.m. ET) on Friday. All crew were reported safe, Marisks said.
The Torkel, a Hong Kong-flagged crude oil tanker, caught fire after being hit in the stern at 5 a.m. UTC on Saturday (midnight ET on Saturday). Less than an hour later, the Arina, also Hong Kong-flagged, was struck in the engine room by a missile.
The attacks demonstrate the “continued critical threat” to commercial shipping in the region, Marisks said, particularly through the “southern corridor” near Oman’s coastline which Iran vehemently opposes.
CNN’s Eleni Giokos, Laura Sharman, Nadeen Ebrahim and Alayna Treene contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Chattahoochee River Bridge inspection prompts closure of several I-285 South lanes
articles.title_zh: Chattahoochee River Bridge inspection prompts closure of several I-285 South lanes
articles.content_orig:
Apparent separation on a bridge near South Cobb Drive in Smyrna forced a full interstate shutdown around 8 p.m. Saturday, triggering hours of delays while crews work on repairs and slowly reopen lanes.
COBB COUNTY, Ga. - An issue with a bridge header joint forced hours of emergency lane closures on Interstate 285 southbound in Smyrna on Saturday, according to state transportation officials.
Around 4:25 p.m. on Saturday, GDOT shut down all southbound lanes of I-285 at State Route 280/South Cobb Drive and diverted traffic off the interstate onto South Cobb Drive after Smyrna police reported that the bridge crossing the Chattahoochee River had separated.
After crews inspected the span and reopened multiple lanes, leaving two right lanes blocked for emergency maintenance, GDOT issued a statement Saturday night clarifying that contractors identified an issue with a bridge header joint on the southbound bridge.
"While there is no structural danger to the bridge, the issue has the potential to impact ride quality for motorists," GDOT said in its release.
Contractors are making a temporary repair Saturday night, and GDOT expects all southbound lanes to reopen no later than 10 p.m. However, as of 11:45 p.m., two right lanes are still blocked and the anticipated reopening time is 5 a.m.
GDOT said contractors are scheduled to begin a long-term fix in early December.
The emergency work adds to an already congested weekend for drivers along the Cobb and Fulton County line.
In a separate, scheduled project just a few miles away, GDOT crews closed the three right lanes of I-285 eastbound over the Chattahoochee River at Powers Ferry Road/Northside Drive (Exit 22) starting at 9 p.m. Friday.
Those eastbound lane closures are scheduled to stay in place until 5 a.m. Monday while crews repair the bridge's concrete overlay, edge beams, substructure and bridge joints.
That $1.6 million preservation project is scheduled to wrap up in late fall 2027.
GDOT has not said what caused the bridge header joint issue to develop Saturday afternoon.
Officials also have not announced exact dates or lane closure plans for the long-term repair scheduled to start in early December.
In the meantime, officials urged drivers to expect delays, reduce their speed and use caution throughout the work zone, and check real-time traffic conditions at 511ga.org or on the Georgia 511 app.
The Source: The information in this story comes from traffic alerts and press releases issued Saturday by the Georgia Department of Transportation and the Smyrna Police Department.

articles.title_orig: Iran unveils dual-missile launcher, new ‘missile city’: What to know
articles.title_zh: Iran unveils dual-missile launcher, new ‘missile city’: What to know
articles.content_orig:
Iran is putting its upgraded missile systems and underground military facilities on display, delivering a defiant message that it still has significant military capabilities despite US-Israeli attacks .
The latest showcase included a dual-missile launcher capable of firing two liquid-fuelled missiles simultaneously, according to state media broadcasting footage of military commanders touring an underground missile facility.
Officials insisted Iran has strengthened its missile and air-defence capabilities since previous rounds of fighting, including the launch of the US-Israel war in late February. Still, Iran is under mounting economic pressure from a naval blockade imposed by the United States that has disrupted its oil exports.
Here’s everything to know about the new dual-missile launcher and Iran’s “missile city”:
Iran has developed a range of ballistic and cruise missiles over the past three decades.
The new dual-missile launcher was unveiled as Major-General Ahmad Vahidi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), toured the underground facility on Saturday.
The IRGC aerospace force flaunted its range of upgraded missiles and military equipment, including the launcher, which is designed to carry and fire two liquid-fuelled missiles simultaneously, according to state broadcaster IRIB.
Liquid-fuelled missiles are launched vertically and offer speed-control capabilities, which can aid in overcoming air defence systems, IRIB reported.
State media said the latest generations of Iranian missiles have improved in range, accuracy and guidance capabilities independent of the US Global Positioning System (GPS).
Vahidi’s tour followed the IRGC aerospace force’s announcement of a new underground facility on November 10, according to the semiofficial Tasnim News Agency.
Tasnim said Iran is constructing underground military complexes able to continue weapons production and storage even under heavy bombardment.
The IRGC has said it transferred its missile and drone production lines from the surface to underground facilities to allow it continuing missile production.
Footage broadcast by IRIB on Saturday showed kilometres of tunnels and hundreds of missiles and launchers, including double launchers, among other systems.
Reporting from Tehran, Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar said it was not clear when the state broadcaster’s footage of the underground site was filmed.
“The IRGC are trying to send a message to the outside world that they are not short of ammunition; they have enough missiles and enough launchers,” he said.
“If the war resumes again, they are going to deploy these capabilities,” he added. “It is a part of their propaganda, but also, Iran is flexing its muscles and trying to restore deterrence.”
Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut, said Iran can safely store spare parts, raw materials and chemicals needed for creating missiles and drones at its underground sites in addition to storing finished missiles and drones.
Iran has been planning for such a scenario for decades, he said. “So there’s no doubt that Iran has stored an enormous amount of all of this,” Khouri, who is also a nonresident senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington DC, told Al Jazeera.
“They’ve shown … they’re prepared to stand sanctions and keep fighting.”
Rob Geist Pinfold, a lecturer in international security at King’s College London, said Iran is now more emboldened than ever to assert its military capabilities due to the outcome of the US midterm elections, in which President Donald Trump’s Republican Party suffered sweeping losses.
The rising cost of living as a result of the war on Iran was a major factor in how people in the US voted in the elections, which saw Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress.
“So [Trump] looks more like the boy who cried wolf,” Pinfold told Al Jazeera. “There seems to be a feeling that the US has been deterred or disincentivised from escalating the conflict.”
Khouri said Iran has taken a gradual approach to showing its technical and military capabilities as well as its political will to strike back.
“[This is] all designed to show the US and Israel … [that] Iran has very sophisticated capabilities that can both evade the Western defence forces and defence systems … and at the same time reach targets that it wants to hit in the countries that it decides to attack,” he said.
At the same time, Iran is suffering under the US naval blockade of its southern ports, so it feels the need to escalate because it feels backed into a corner, Pinfold noted.
He added that Iran’s economy is already in recession and there are growing fears it could suffer an even bigger hit.
“Very little if any oil is coming out of Iran at the moment,” Pinfold said.

articles.title_orig: Social Security benefits are rising in 2027, but other changes could affect what you keep
articles.title_zh: Social Security benefits are rising in 2027, but other changes could affect what you keep
articles.content_orig:
Whether you're working or retired, changes to Social Security in 2027 could affect your finances.
Starting in January, millions of program beneficiaries will get a 3.6% increase to their benefits, thanks to the annual cost-of-living adjustment. But rising Medicare premiums could chip away at the increase — and as beneficiaries' incomes rise, that may affect the taxes they owe and their eligibility for a new senior deduction.
Meanwhile, a higher taxable earnings cap means some workers will pay Social Security taxes on more income, reducing their paycheck.
Here's a breakdown of what to expect in the new year.
Social Security's limit for payroll taxes is adjusted every year to reflect the average wage index.
In 2027, the taxable maximum will go up to $192,300 in earnings, up from $184,500 in 2026. Workers and employers each pay a 6.2% payroll tax on earnings up to that limit — or 12.4% for self-employed workers. Medicare taxes of 1.45% for both workers and employers are not subject to a limit.
In 2027, workers who earn $192,300 or more will pay $11,922.60 in total Social Security payroll taxes, according to the Social Security Administration, while self-employed workers will pay $23,845.20.
"If you're somebody whose income is over what the new threshold is going to be, this increase in the threshold results in a tax increase to you," said Tim Steffen, director of advanced planning at financial services firm Baird.
The 3.6% Social Security cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 is slated to increase retirement benefits by about $75 per month on average, according to the Social Security Administration.
The annual adjustment is the largest boost to benefits since 2023 due to rising inflation. The COLA averaged 2.6% from 2000 to 2026, according to the Senior Citizens League , a nonpartisan senior group.
Around 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will see benefit increases, according to the agency.
The maximum benefit for a worker at full retirement age — when individuals become eligible for 100% of the benefits they've earned — will rise to $4,188 per month in 2027, up from $4,152 per month in 2026, according to the federal agency. To be eligible for the maximum benefit at full retirement age — typically age 66 to 67 — you generally have to earn up to the taxable threshold for each of your working years factored into the calculation.
How much of the COLA increase Social Security beneficiaries see depends in part on their Medicare premiums, which may be deducted directly from benefit checks.
Monthly rates are poised to increase for both Medicare Part B, which covers medically necessary services and preventive care, and Part D, which provides prescription drug coverage.
The standard monthly Medicare Part B premium will be $209.40 in 2027 — a $6.50 increase from $202.90 in 2026, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
"It's not often that we see a Part B [premium] increase that is lower than the COLA," Mary Johnson, an independent Social Security and Medicare policy analyst, said of the 3.2% increase. The last time that happened was in 2023, she said.
Medicare Part D beneficiaries may also pay higher premiums in 2027.
Assuming enrollees keep the same plan, the average enrollment-weighted monthly Part D premium may be $51 in 2027, up 50% from $34 in 2026, according to projections from KFF, a provider of health policy research and polling. That is higher than CMS' projections, which forecast the national average premium for standalone Part D plans will rise about $1, to $36, in 2027 from $35 in 2026.
Standard monthly premiums for Part B and plan-specific premiums for Part D apply to individuals who have $112,000 or less in modified adjusted gross income, or $224,000 for married couples. Beneficiaries with higher income pay larger premiums because of income-related monthly adjustment amounts, which affect 9% of Medicare Part B and Part D beneficiaries, according to CMS.
With bigger Social Security benefits, more households may find that some portion of benefits is taxable — though a new senior deduction may help provide some relief to those who are eligible.
Social Security benefits may be subject to federal income taxes for certain individuals. The thresholds at which those taxes are applied are not adjusted from year to year.
Whether or not benefits are taxed is determined by a formula known as combined income — the sum of adjusted gross income, tax-exempt interest income and half of Social Security benefits:
Individuals who are subject to taxes may opt to withhold taxes from their Social Security benefit checks, rather than face a potential bill during tax filing season.
Separately, a temporary senior deduction of up to $6,000 for individuals ages 65 and over may help to indirectly reduce taxes on Social Security benefits.
That deduction, part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025, helps reduce retirees' taxable income, according to Steffen. It's in place through 2028. Because the break phases out for individuals with modified adjusted gross income starting at $75,000 — and for married couples with $150,000 — it's important to watch your income if you're close to those limits, Steffen said.
"Keep in mind that if you're over 65, you might qualify for this deduction," Steffen said. "But if you let your income get too big, you might lose the deduction."
Moreover, any extra income that causes you to lose the deduction may also come with its own taxes, making it more expensive, according to Steffen.
"What we've been telling our clients is that tax planning is a lot more complicated than it used to be, and you can't do it on the back of an envelope anymore," he said. "You need to use good tools that can do good calculations for you."
Individuals who claim Social Security retirement benefits before their full retirement age and who continue to work may be subject to withholdings.
In 2027, individuals under full retirement age may earn up to $25,560 per year, up from $24,480 in 2026, without adjustments to their Social Security benefits. For every $2 in earnings above that limit, $1 in Social Security benefits will be withheld.
Importantly, those withholdings are not lost completely. Once a beneficiary reaches full retirement age, the withheld money will be credited to their benefits over their remaining lifespan.
In the year individuals reach full retirement age, the retirement earnings test limit is higher — $67,920 per year in 2027, up from $65,160 per year in 2026. For every $3 in earnings above that limit, $1 in Social Security benefits is withheld.
Starting the month a beneficiary reaches full retirement age, no earnings are withheld.

articles.title_orig: Russian cargo ship set ablaze in Baltic Sea drifts into Gulf of Finland
articles.title_zh: Russian cargo ship set ablaze in Baltic Sea drifts into Gulf of Finland
articles.content_orig:
Finland says work is continuing on the Sparta II ship on Sunday
Rescue and firefighting efforts are continuing for a Russian cargo vessel hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, authorities have said.
The ship - the Sparta II - was bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday that work was ongoing to make sure the cargo ship did not sink but it was not aware of any danger to surrounding maritime traffic.
Water was still being used to douse the ship on Sunday, and Finland said Estonian and Russian assets were also involved in recovery work.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used in the strike, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."
The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.
It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Defence Minister Antti HÃ¤kkÃ¤nen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland .

articles.title_orig: Russian Warship Explosion in Libya Destroys Corvette Merkury
articles.title_zh: Russian Warship Explosion in Libya Destroys Corvette Merkury
articles.content_orig:
An explosion has occurred on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port after a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.
The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.
It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.
Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
GNS said the country was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
Seperately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.

articles.title_orig: Russian attack near Ukraine's capital strikes apartment building, killing 2 and wounding 4 others
articles.title_zh: Russian attack near Ukraine's capital strikes apartment building, killing 2 and wounding 4 others
articles.content_orig:
A Russian drone strike partially destroyed a five-story apartment building near Kyiv, leaving 14 people unaccounted for, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday.
Rescuers were searching the rubble in Dymer, north of Kyiv, where part of the building collapsed and a fire broke out. Nine people had been evacuated, Zelenskyy added, warning that others could remain trapped.
The attack prompted the Ukrainian president to renew pressure on Washington to approve deliveries of U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles financed by Ukraine’s allies, amid mounting Russian aerial attacks. “It is particularly difficult to understand the delays in supplying anti-ballistic interceptors to Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said on X .
He urged Washington to authorize the transfer of Patriot missiles already paid for by Ukraine’s partners through NATO’s PURL program , which allows allies to purchase American weapons for Kyiv.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said earlier this month that deliveries under the program, including Patriots, were continuing.
Russia launched 186 drones overnight, including 72 jet-powered models, Ukraine’s air force said. Ukrainian defenses shot down or disabled 161, while strikes were recorded at 18 locations.
Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked 20 Ukrainian regions over the past week, launching around 2,700 drones, nearly 1,460 aerial bombs and 165 missiles.
Many were ballistic missiles, including North Korean-made weapons, he said, accusing Moscow of helping Pyongyang improve their accuracy.

articles.title_orig: 26-year-old Google worker earns $323,000 a year—but lives on less than minimum wage
articles.title_zh: 26-year-old Google worker earns $323,000 a year—but lives on less than minimum wage
articles.content_orig:
This story is part of CNBC Make It's Millennial Money series, which details how people around the world earn, spend and save their money.
At 26 years old, Google AI security analyst and YouTuber Charles Broomfield is on track to earn about $323,000 this year — but he lives on less than minimum wage.
For the past few years, Broomfield has kept his annual spending on core living expenses under $20,000, less than the roughly $23,700 a full-time worker would earn at the minimum wage, averaged across all 50 states.
He does it by living with roommates in Washington, D.C., walking or biking instead of driving, eating free meals at work and rarely spending beyond his basic needs. Even when he splurges on something fun, he keeps things modest; in August, that meant a baseball game and a single $7 beer.
"I guess something else that probably does make me a little bit unique is I really don't feel joy when I buy things," he says. "I feel like I have what I need."
There is a goal behind all that saving. Broomfield has pursued financial independence since college and now expects to reach his target of $750,000 in investments within the next year, well ahead of his original goal of doing so by age 30. As his income has climbed, his lifestyle has largely stayed the same, he says.
Here's how Broomfield keeps his spending so low and what he plans to do once he no longer needs the paycheck.
Broomfield grew up in Colorado Springs, Colorado, the son of two military veterans. He and his siblings had to set aside half of everything they earned growing up. They could spend the other half or earn interest from their parents by putting that money away, too.
By his teenage years, Broomfield had become a disciplined saver. At the time, he dreamed of using his cash stash to buy some of the familiar trappings of wealth.
"I wanted a Lamborghini and I wanted some nice penthouse," he says. "I just wanted them because I thought other people wanted them."
At 17, Broomfield discovered Mr. Money Mustache, a personal finance blog by a former software engineer who retired at 30. The blog advocates living frugally and investing much of your income to build a portfolio large enough to support you through withdrawals, without needing a paycheck. It introduced Broomfield to the financial independence, retire early — or FIRE — movement and gave all that saving a new purpose.
"All I had to do was live super frugally and I could actually reach financial freedom by the time I was 30 and go do whatever actually made me happy in life," he says.
The idea stuck with him. After graduating from Knox College in 2022, Broomfield moved to Northern Virginia for a job paying more than $100,000 a year and set a goal of reaching $750,000 in investments before 30 while spending less than $25,000 a year.
He also decided to start at $0. Broomfield had roughly $50,000 in savings when he graduated, with his parents having covered the portion of his college tuition not paid for by scholarships. He wanted his FIRE total to reflect only what he earned after college.
In his first year after college, Broomfield was "super geeked out" about reaching financial freedom, he says.
"It's almost the only thing I thought about, because I was building all these new habits and making real money for really the first time in my life," he says.
That enthusiasm sometimes took him to extremes. He even considered living in a van parked in his employer's garage to avoid paying rent.
"I crunched the numbers on it, and effectively every year that I spent living in a van rather than paying rent would allow me to retire approximately one month faster," he says. "It just [didn't] seem really worth it to go to that extreme."
But Broomfield still found satisfaction in squeezing every dollar out of his budget. He once biked two miles to a grocery store to save $1 on toothpaste rather than buy it at the Whole Foods next to his apartment.
"For a lot of people, they feel their wins by buying stuff for themselves," Broomfield says. "I get my wins by seeing how much I can invest."
Looking back, Broomfield acknowledges that some of his early efforts to save money made little difference in how quickly he could reach financial independence.
"I never expect anybody else to do exactly what I'm doing," he says. "I know I'm way more of a geek about this than most people, and I'm particularly well positioned to be able to live this kind of life."
Broomfield's core living expenses totaled $1,477 in August, excluding savings, investments and payments toward his graduate school tuition.
Here's a breakdown of where his money went that month, including those additional payments:
Roughly 90% of Broomfield's income went to savings and investments in August, a fairly typical month for him, he says. He put about $7,931 into his 401(k) and another $10,000 into a taxable brokerage account.
Another $700 went toward a 0% interest employer tuition repayment plan with a former employer, leaving him with a remaining balance of $16,800 in August.
Housing is Broomfield's biggest expense, though he keeps costs down by sharing an apartment with four roommates. In a neighborhood where one-bedroom apartments commonly rent for more than $2,000, the arrangement saves him about $1,000 a month.
One thing Broomfield is willing to splurge on is a martial arts gym membership. He pays $229 a month to train as a kickboxer, even though he could work out for free at Google's office gym. Broomfield considers it a "young person's sport" and doesn't want to postpone competing until after he reaches financial independence. It's also a way to socialize with other amateur fighters who share his interest.
Broomfield doesn't own a car and generally walks, bikes or takes public transportation. Google covers his daily Metro commute, which helps keep his transportation costs low. He tries to meet friends near Metro stations and, when visiting his grandfather in Virginia, takes public transit as far as he can before using Uber for the last leg of the trip.
Before joining Google, Broomfield typically spent around $200 a month on food. Now that he eats most of his meals at work , he spends about $70 a month on average. His $28 food bill in August was especially low because he had ingredients left over from July.
He also cooks less at home these days. Previously, he relied more on batch cooking, including pressure cooker chili that makes nine servings for about $2 each. For snacks, he might have a bowl of Raisin Bran or celery with peanut butter.
“I did the math once, and peanut butter was the lowest cost thing per gram of protein in the entire grocery store,” he says in a video on his YouTube channel, which he started in 2023 to document his FIRE journey.
For entertainment, he relies on the free version of YouTube, where he watches educational content about startups, business and entrepreneurship, or listens to music.
Broomfield expects to make about $323,000 in 2026, more than triple the roughly $100,000 he earned in his first year out of college. His compensation rose to about $120,000 over his first three years, then jumped to $200,000 when he joined Amazon Web Services in 2025. After a brief stint at Capital One, he moved to Google this year. By keeping his expenses low, investing most of what he earns and riding an upward-trending stock market, he has built up about $650,000 in investments since graduating from college.
Broomfield earns money from his YouTube channel as well, which has expanded to offer personal finance and career advice. About $48,000 of his projected income this year will come from the channel and a related career-coaching business.
Even as his income has grown, Broomfield has stuck with roommates, public transportation and the same modest spending habits.
"I've really separated how happy I am from how much money I spend," he says. "I truly don't believe that I would be significantly happier if I spent a lot more money."

articles.title_orig: GTA 6 Glitch Unlocks The FPS On Xbox Series X|S, But With Multiple Drawbacks
articles.title_zh: GTA 6 Glitch Unlocks The FPS On Xbox Series X|S, But With Multiple Drawbacks
articles.content_orig:
If there's anything we could add to GTA 6 as things stand, it'd be an official 60FPS mode. That's obviously not possible right now due to how demanding the game is on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S hardware, even in the case of the PS5 Pro.
Interestingly though, over the weekend, players have discovered the ability to activate what some are calling a "60FPS Glitch" or "60FPS Bug" on Xbox consoles, forcing the game to unlock its FPS and run at a higher frame rate than it's actually supposed to.
Someone called Meowwie64 on Reddit appears to have found this, and here's what they did to activate it:
Now, as mentioned, there are multiple drawbacks here. The first one is that the glitch speeds up most aspects of the game, making it run faster than intended (and look like it's in fast-forward mode!). This is obviously not an ideal way to enjoy GTA 6, and serves as an immediate deal-breaker in my view.
Another one is that reaching 60FPS is pretty much impossible under normal gameplay circumstances. If you're driving down a highway, for example, you're likely only going to get around 35-40FPS at max, with 60FPS and above being saved for situations that require no graphical intensity whatsoever.
And finally, it should be noted that GTA 6 was never intended to be run this way on Xbox Series X|S, and therefore you could run into all sorts of issues - crashes, bugs, maybe even your console overheating. That last one is unlikely, but the game has been specifically built to run at 30FPS on these machines, so it's not worth pushing it in our view.
We'll leave you with some footage of this glitch running on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S down below (courtesy of the always-excellent Fuzion Xbox Testing ), and prepare for it to be officially fixed in an upcoming GTA 6 update.

articles.title_orig: Strong Earnings Prove No Match for the Crumbling AI Trade
articles.title_zh: Strong Earnings Prove No Match for the Crumbling AI Trade
articles.content_orig:
Stocks got hit hard this week amid fears that the AI trade could be buckling. Spencer Platt/Getty Images hide caption
A yearslong AI boom showed signs of unraveling this week in spectacular fashion.
AI-related stocks have powered markets to record highs and helped support the broader economy. But investors now fear that a potential bubble in the sector could be bursting, which could spark wider financial repercussions.
Here's what to know about the week in AI and why alarm bells are ringing
Investors were hoping the stock market debut of AI giant Anthropic this week would provide a boost to the markets. Instead, the entire stock market got pummeled on Friday, sparking one of the worst weeks that Wall Street has seen in quite some time.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 10% for the week, its worst performance since the onset of COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns in March 2020. Even Anthropic, which gained 17% on its debut, ended up slumping more than 8% to close near its IPO price on Friday.
Meanwhile, both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average entered a correction as of the close of trade on Friday, meaning a drop of 10% from their recent highs.
It's the culmination of weeks of fears that have been building up about the sustainability of the AI trade.
Back in September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years. That poses a big challenge to AI companies because they still need to borrow billions of dollars to do things like build out data centers that power the growth of their technologies. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for them.
Democrats also took over both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, vowing to take a tougher regulatory approach toward the AI sector and slow down the build-out of data centers, which have been unpopular with voters .
Democrats were also elected as governors in states that have been key to the data center build-out, like Texas, where Gina Hinojosa stunned the political world by winning her race .
And then there's the turmoil at Nvidia, the top AI chip company. Its CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned this month after being suspected of having had an affair with a woman who's believed to have been spying for China.
All this has exacerbated investors' worries about the sustainability of an AI trade into which investors have sunk billions of dollars.
Hank Smith, the head of investment strategy at Haverford Trust, thinks it's unlikely the markets will recover quickly, the way they have previously bounced right back after AI shares dropped.
"I think it has taken the market the better part of the last two or three weeks to realize it is not going to be like the previous sell-offs," Smith said, adding that AI could fall "out of favor" through next year.
"It's just going to take a little bit of time to heal," he said of the tech market.
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO this month, throwing the company's leadership into turmoil. Here, Huang delivers a keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas on Jan. 6, 2025. Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
That has been a big source of debate on Wall Street.
Some people fear that the AI sector could be in the middle of a bubble that is bursting, just like tech stocks did during the dot-com bust of 2000. At the time, investors had sunk money into tech companies that often had no profits — and not even revenues — and were wiped out in the bust.
Smith, though, argues that this time around the AI trade is being powered by top companies such as Meta and Apple, and he doesn't see them as likely to go out of business, the way many dot-coms did. Nvidia — despite its leadership shake-up — still posted strong results this week.
The future prospects for AI, Smith said, are "not based on a pie in the sky."
That said, Smith continued, there is still a question about whether investors will see the sizable returns they are hoping to get.
And there's another big fear: how interconnected AI companies have become. Nvidia, for example, not only owns shares in other big AI companies like Anthropic but is also lending a lot of money to them. In turn, they are buying chips from Nvidia.
This circular system of financing also involves lesser-known companies, such as CoreWeave, that are borrowing heavily to build out data centers. Nvidia is a major investor in CoreWeave, in another sign of the interconnectedness .
This close-knit ecosystem is raising concerns that if one or two companies run into trouble, it could kick off a chain reaction that could lead to something like a financial crisis.
It could be potentially significant. The U.S. economy has effectively become an AI economy.
Building out data centers, for example, may be unpopular with voters, but construction creates jobs, which is why some parts of the U.S. have courted the centers. In fact, AI investments helped the economy grow at an annual rate of 3.4% in the most recent quarter.
Not only that, but AI-related stocks have become an integral part of the broader markets, accounting for a substantial portion of the S&P 500. That means many investors hold these stocks as part of their portfolios, including as components of index funds, pensions or retirement funds like 401(k)s.
So if the AI trade unravels, it could have a ripple effect far beyond the high-tech world.

Oops, something went wrong
Technology shares nosedived on Friday and dragged stocks into the red around the world, after AI firm Anthropic's bumper market debut failed to dispel growing worries about the sector's massive investments and sky-high valuations.
Anthropic shares briefly rocketed from an initial offering price of $83 to over $110 on Thursday despite a broader sell-off on Wall Street, but fell back sharply with the price plunging back below $89 at the close on Friday.
"The performance of the shares over the coming days and weeks could provide one of the clearest tests yet of whether investors believe the enormous sums being poured into AI will ultimately generate attractive returns," said Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell.
While Anthropic surged on its Nasdaq debut, the tech-dominated index struggled on Friday, closing down more than five percent.
New York's broader S&P 500, which also trades the shares of the world's biggest tech companies, shed 3.7 percent on Friday, extending a run of losses.
"The disappointing performance has reinforced concerns about elevated AI valuations and the enormous capital commitments required to support the industry's growth," said Briefing.com analysts in a note.
"Neither Anthropic's IPO nor Nvidia's strong earnings has been sufficient to restore confidence, with investors continuing to sell into rebound attempts.
James Reilly of Capital Economics said the fall in tech stocks could "have further to run."
He labelled the prospect of an "AI bust in 2027" his central forecast and a growing worry for investors.
"This doesn't mean we think the technology is a dud, nor that demand will collapse. But the revenue hurdle to justify the scale of AI investment looks very demanding," he wrote.
Traders have also been spooked by the US Commerce Department's move to close a loophole allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia's powerful AI chips remotely, adding to worries that a new Democratic-led Congress will impose further restrictions on the sector.
It comes after Nvidia's high-profile founder and CEO Jensen Huang had to resign following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.
The chip giant, which has endured a long period of losses, slumped by 14.01 percent at the close in New York on Friday, despite posting massive profits earlier in the week.
In Asian trading Friday, the Tokyo, Seoul and Taipei stock markets -- home to the region's leading AI-linked firms -- tumbled between five and 6.2 percent.
Europe's main stock markets all fell back significantly by close of trading, with shares in French video game maker Ubisoft slumping more than 20 percent after it posted a bigger first-half loss than expected.
The report came amid the worldwide hype surrounding "Grand Theft Auto VI", the latest in the hugely popular Rockstar Games series, which took a record $3.79 billion in opening day retail sales this week.
