articles.title_orig: Delta says ‘automation’ issues causing delays in Atlanta, nationwide
articles.title_zh: Delta says ‘automation’ issues causing delays in Atlanta, nationwide
articles.content_orig:
ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — Delays are mounting across the country for Delta Air Lines flights after a ground stop and ground delay caused by a technical issue, the Atlanta-based airline said.
A ground stop issued Sunday morning for Delta flights on their way to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport turned into a ground delay, the FAA said Sunday.
The ground delay, which is in effect until at least 1 p.m., means that flights on the ground heading to Atlanta will now be allowed to depart, but they are being delayed nearly an hour.
The ground delays are due to a problem with Delta’s weight and balance automation system, the Atlanta-based airline said.
“Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” the airline said.
Because flights are taking longer to depart due to Delta personnel having to manually calculate their weight, it is limiting gate space for arriving flights, exacerbating the delays.
“We are working with our air traffic control counterparts to strategically enact programs to protect airport gates and tarmac areas from congestion at our Atlanta hub,” Delta said.
Delta passengers are reporting delays at multiple US airports online, including Atlanta, Newark, LaGuardia, Reagan National, Dulles, Boston, Baltimore, Miami, Minneapolis, Nashville, San Antonio, Birmingham.
Just before 10 a.m., nearly 500 flights were delayed at the airport, according to FlightAware , a flight tracking website.
The delays come just as the busy Thanksgiving travel period is about to begin. Officials at Hartsfield-Jackson airport expect more than 4 million passengers through Dec. 1, up 5% from last year.
READ: Hartsfield-Jackson airport expects 4 million passengers during Thanksgiving holiday travel
Just days ago, a nationwide ground stop caused mass cancellations at the world’s busiest airport.
Atlanta’s airport General Manager Ricky Smith said the nationwide ground stop told Atlanta News First that the incident was a “big test” as Thanksgiving travel nears.
This is a developing story. Stay with Atlanta News First as we learn more.

articles.title_orig: Correction or deeper reckoning? Investors seek signs US stock selling will abate
articles.title_zh: Correction or deeper reckoning? Investors seek signs US stock selling will abate
articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 lost 8.6% this week and closed 6% below its 200-day average. Earnings haven’t cracked, which makes this a liquidity event. The question is whether the Fed blinks before the break hardens.
Last week, in VIX Spike: Complacency’s Bill Coming Due , we warned that low volatility eventually begets high volatility. That bill came due early. The S&P 500 fell 8.6% to 6,910, its seventh straight losing session and the longest losing streak since February 2020. The Nasdaq-100 dropped 10.4%, the Dow lost 8.0%, and the Russell 2000 slid 7.5%. At 11.6% below its October 6 record, the index is in “correction” territory, and the VIX nearly doubled to 37.
So was this a liquidation of leveraged positions due to margin calls? Partly, but not the way the headlines suggest. FINRA’s latest data put margin debt at $1.45 trillion in October, down 2.1% from September and 3.6% below June’s record. Margin borrowing was already easing before the week began.
What we saw instead was mechanical deleveraging. On Thursday, just 38 S&P 500 stocks rose while 464 fell, and all 11 sectors finished lower, even staples. Goldman’s Rich Privorotsky called it “a pretty violent liquidation” in a note covered by ZeroHedge. Dealers were heavily short gamma into Friday’s monthly options expiration, which fed the afternoon selling. Desk chatter also had investors selling gold, copper, crypto and Nvidia to fund allocations in Anthropic’s IPO , which priced at $83 on Wednesday. Gold fell 9.5%, copper 10.2% and Bitcoin broke below $60,000.
Macro supplied the trigger. Fed Governor Christopher Waller called for a 50-basis-point hike at the December 8-9 meeting after a third straight 0.3% monthly gain in core CPI. The Commerce Department’s rule restricting remote access to advanced AI chips by Chinese firms took effect on Thursday, landing on the AI supply chain the same day. Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.91% from 5.15%. The bond market is starting to price a growth problem, while the Fed is still fighting an inflation problem.
Here is the real question that needs an answer. “Have the fundamentals changed?” Not yet. Through FactSet’s November 13 update, analysts had raised fourth-quarter EPS estimates 1.1% since September 30, something that rarely happens mid-quarter, and third-quarter earnings grew 31.9%.
The Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow still tracks fourth-quarter growth at 3.4%, and initial jobless claims of 203,000 remain near historic lows. Cracks are showing only at the edges. The Philadelphia Fed index collapsed to 6.3 against expectations of 20, the Conference Board’s leading index fell 0.3%, and existing home sales hit their slowest pace since 2010. So far, this is a valuation and liquidity event, not an earnings recession. At 6,910, the S&P 500 trades near 16.6 times FactSet’s November 5 forward earnings estimate of $415.82, down from 17.7 times on that date.
This suggests that the liquidation of positions is likely “overdone.” Since 1950, the S&P 500 has suffered 17 separate episodes in which it fell 8% or more over five sessions. It was higher three months later in 15 of them, with a median gain of 8.1% . The catch is that the median further drawdown along the way was 4.5%, so the bottom rarely arrives on schedule.
Next week, the main focus will be on the Federal Reserve. If Wednesday’s PCE data cools and Fed speakers soften, the setup for a reflexive rally is in place. If not, Privorotsky’s 2018 comparison, when the Fed kept hiking and stocks didn’t bottom until Christmas Eve , becomes the playbook .
The S&P 500 closed Friday, November 20, at 6,910.39, down 8.6% for the week. That leaves the index 6.0% below its 200-day average at 7,348.58 and 9.4% below its 50-day average at 7,625.25. It closed below the lower 2-standard-deviation Bollinger Band at 7,094. It also finished just 18 points above the lower 3-SD band at 6,892. To wit: the index ended the week 2.9 standard deviations below its 20-day mean.
The technical backdrop is telling a more interesting story. First, momentum is confirming the extreme selling pressure this past week. On Friday, the 14-day RSI fell to 24.7. That is its lowest reading since April 8, 2025. That date is important as it marked the bottom of the tariff-driven selloff. Notably, during that selloff, the market was being priced for an impact on earnings growth from tariffs. However, currently, analysts continue to maintain or raise earnings estimates for the fourth quarter and next year.
Secondly, the MACD sits at −130 index points, well below its signal line at −75, and Williams %R is at −97. Such is what a forced-selling week looks like on a chart. Oversold is a condition, not a buy signal, and it can persist longer than anyone expects during a liquidation.
Third, breadth tells a more nuanced story. The equal-weight S&P 500 fell 6.1% against 8.4% for the cap-weighted S&P 500 index. The damage has been largely concentrated in the AI complex, with Technology falling 12.3%. However,  semiconductors (SMH) dropped 17.8%, while Nvidia lost 22.9%.
Even the more defensive sectors couldn’t avoid the selling pressure. Staples and Utilities lost 2.0% and 3.0%, respectively. In other words, defensive stocks did their job of reducing the volatility, but they didn’t avoid it. The average stock is in better shape than the index, which helps any rebound broaden. But leadership is what broke, and leadership rarely heals in a week.
Volatility and bonds tell you what kind of selloff this is. The VIX closed at 37.24, nearly double last Friday’s 19.30. Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury yield fell 24 basis points, and the long-bond ETF (TLT) gained 2.6% while nearly everything else fell. When bonds rally as stocks drop, investors are running from risk rather than scrambling for cash. Watch that relationship next week. If Treasuries start selling off alongside stocks, the liquidation has moved into a more dangerous phase.
In our portfolios, we used the decline to nibble on NVDA and PANW this week. However, these were very small additions, and something that we will likely continue to do into further weakness. Notably, these are NOT calls that the market has bottomed. Next week, we’ll trim value positions to raise cash. That keeps the dip buys from adding to overall equity exposure while the index sits below a level that matters this much. Our 7,000 risk line gave way on Friday, and we’re treating it that way.
For more aggressive traders, the playbook is to let the rubber band snap before acting. With the market at a 2.9-standard deviation (SD) extreme, a reflexive rally toward the lower 2-SD band near 7,094 should be expected. That is a tradeable reflex rally, but should be treated as a strict trade with defined exits.
The 200-day average at 7,349 is the first real test above the market currently. For now, use any rallies into that zone to rebalance and reduce risk rather than chase. However, on the downside, the 3-SD band at 6,892 is only a thin level of support. Any decisive break opens the April 7 close of 6,617, where the spring rally launched.
Next week, there is only one market level that really matters: 7,349. Any snapback toward the 200-day average would be normal from an oversold extreme this deep. What matters is whether the index can close and hold above it. That action will decide whether this break joins the healed ones or the deep breaks that keep going.
This coming week, Thanksgiving will compress everything into just three trading sessions. Markets are closed on Thursday, and then the market will close early at 1:00 p.m. ET on Friday. For investors, this is a week to turn off monitors and enjoy your family, as the thin holiday trading tends to magnify moves in both directions. With the VIX sitting at 37, this is where investors tend to make mistakes.

articles.title_orig: A Physicist Built a Black Hole on a Chip. Then It Started to Leak.
articles.title_zh: A Physicist Built a Black Hole on a Chip. Then It Started to Leak.
articles.content_orig:
Black holes do many things.
They sit in space, slurping up matter, drawing spacetime around them like a cozy blanket, and firing off powerful jets of near-light-speed plasma.
What they are not especially good at is letting go.
But when physicist Antonino Flachi of Keio University in Japan built an analog black hole on a chip, something strange happened at its tiny event horizon – something that, in a real black hole, would be forbidden by the laws of general relativity.
When he poked a hole – metaphorically speaking – the black hole began to leak.
It's an experiment that offers physicists a new tool for probing which properties of black holes are universal – and which might change when the rules of physics do.
"Digital circuits thus form a reconfigurable class of gravitational analogs," Flachi writes in a preprint (yet to undergo peer review) uploaded to arXiv , "and realize an analog black hole as a cellular automaton."
Their penchant for absorbing light and letting nothing detectable escape from within their event horizons means they're invisible to most of the tools we use for studying the cosmos – telescopes that rely on the electromagnetic spectrum.
However, the mathematics describing the behavior of black holes can be used to build laboratory experiments that replicate some of their properties and behaviors so that we can study what they are capable of .
One way to do this is with sound.
Sound waves traveling through a moving fluid can behave in ways very similar to light traveling through the curved spacetime around a black hole. If the fluid flows inward faster than sound can travel outward, the sound waves become trapped, unable to escape the current.
This creates what physicists call an acoustic black hole.
But what if you could build an acoustic black hole without all the mess and fuss of speakers, fluids, and currents?
This is what Flachi has done, replacing the entire kit and kaboodle with a compact digital circuit.
"We have built an analog black hole out of logic gates," he writes .
"Its horizon is a property not of the wiring but of the state: a closed curve in a lattice of 32-bit words along which the emergent flow carries disturbances inward exactly as fast as they spread outward."
He calls his system a 'digital acoustic black hole', a circuit that contains a grid of cells, each storing information as a series of bits – the ones and zeros that form the basis of digital computing. The grid stored a total of around 604 million bits.
At each tick of a clock, logic gates update the information in each cell according to a set of rules based on fluid dynamics, creating the digital equivalent of water flowing inward toward a drain.
These rules also govern how disturbances travel through the grid. Where the simulated flow carries those disturbances inward as fast as they can travel outward, an acoustic event horizon emerges.
Unlike a physical fluid, which can be unpredictable and difficult to control, the precisely defined rules for the digital acoustic black hole make the digital fluid far more controllable. Experiments can even be repeated under identical conditions, right down to the individual bits.
To test his creation, Flachi measured five properties of the simulated black hole: the stability of its event horizon, the horizon itself, the way disturbances propagate through it, its response to being disturbed (the ringdown), and a phenomenon called superradiance, in which waves can gain energy from a rotating black hole.
It performed brilliantly. The event horizon remained stable for 3 hours, and the circuit demonstrated ringdown and superradiance, consistent with the mathematical predictions.
But then, Flachi got curious. He wanted to know what would happen if he changed one small thing.
Inside the event horizon, he flipped just one of the system's 604 million bits – and it was as though the black hole had sprung a leak.
Flipping the bit created an acoustic disturbance in the black hole. Most of it remained contained beyond the event horizon – as you would expect for something taking place behind that boundary.
But a small fraction of the disturbance escaped, carried by short-wavelength waves that could travel faster than the effective speed of sound in the circuit.
So the event horizon worked as expected for longer waves, but was not quite so impenetrable to shorter ones.
And the deeper inside the horizon Flachi flipped the bit, the less of the disturbance escaped. The leakage diminished exponentially with distance from the boundary.
This doesn't mean that real black holes have leaky event horizons – but it reveals something important about black hole analogs. The behavior of their horizons isn't necessarily universal, but can depend on the underlying physics of the system in which they emerge.
And Flachi's system offers a new way to poke them. He has shown that a functioning black hole analog can be built entirely out of digital logic – one whose underlying rules are precisely known and finely controllable.
This means that it can be used to probe the physics of black hole horizons, and to explore new scenarios that reveal what might be possible if the rules of physics were bent just a teeny tiny iota.
The paper has not yet been peer-reviewed, but a preprint is available on arXiv .

articles.title_orig: US ports face cyber attack onslaught as hackers target vital trade routes
articles.title_zh: US ports face cyber attack onslaught as hackers target vital trade routes
articles.content_orig:
Hackers are stepping up attacks on U.S. ports and cargo ships, targeting computer systems that keep goods and energy exports moving.
The attacks have intensified in recent months, with breaches reported at ports, aboard oil tankers, and at a major shipping company, Financial Times reported on Sunday.
The chief executive of the nation's largest crude oil export hub, the Port of Corpus Christi in Texas, says his port faces hundreds or even thousands of attempted intrusions each day.
At Corpus Christi, which handles about 2.3 million barrels of crude oil exports a day, hackers have probed networks and sent messages impersonating senior executives to trick employees into granting access.
"They're poking at our systems and trying to find vulnerabilities," Port of Corpus Christi CEO Kent Britton said. "With AI, it'll only get more complicated."
Corpus Christi is preparing to hire its fourth cybersecurity staff member and is seeking additional help from Washington.
If an attack takes its systems offline, tugboats can escort vessels through parts of the channel, and the harbor master's office can use two-way radios, binoculars, and paper records to keep traffic moving.
Britton said some of the attempts came from states and organizations known for malicious activity. He declined to identify them.
The FBI recently warned that hackers are using artificial intelligence to automate attacks.
The U.S. Coast Guard said increasingly connected computer networks and equipment controls mean a breach can shut a terminal gate, interrupt cargo handling, or disrupt ship systems, putting crews and supply chains at risk.
An Aug. 4 cyberattack disrupted operations at all three North Carolina Ports facilities, in Wilmington, Morehead City, and Charlotte, WECT in Wilmington, North Carolina, reported.
The agency activated its cybersecurity contingency plan and brought in state and federal partners, including the Coast Guard.
"In Wilmington, the operations team implemented a delayed opening and transitioned to manual gate processing, allowing the IT team to focus on system recovery efforts," a North Carolina Ports spokesperson told the station.
The agency contained the breach and began restoring its systems.
At the time of WECT's report, officials had yet to identify who was responsible or give a timeline for full restoration.
The spokesperson said there was no indication sensitive data had been compromised.
The Coast Guard reported a 17% increase in maritime cyber incidents last year.
In August, the agency and the FBI boarded two foreign-flagged tankers after indications their networks had been compromised near the Strait of Gibraltar.
The vessels were carrying crude oil and liquefied petroleum gas from the Mediterranean to Galveston, Texas.
Investigators have yet to publicly identify suspects.
The Port of Los Angeles said it blocked 120 million attempted attacks in August, including automated attempts, nearly double its monthly average in 2023.
Shipping company Maersk said hackers stole data in a breach this month and that its operations continued without disruption.
The Coast Guard issued maritime cybersecurity rules in 2025 requiring covered operators to report qualifying cyber incidents to the National Response Center and provide annual training to personnel with access to computer networks or equipment controls.
The rules cover U.S.-flagged vessels and maritime facilities, including facilities on the Outer Continental Shelf, that already must maintain Coast Guard-approved security plans.
By July 16, 2027, covered owners and operators must designate a cybersecurity officer, complete an assessment, and submit a cybersecurity plan to the Coast Guard for approval.
"Early preparation is absolutely critical," said Rear Adm. Robert Compher, the Coast Guard's assistant commandant for prevention policy.
The agency said it also checks for cyber risks during inspections of foreign-flagged ships.
In serious cases, it can detain a vessel, deny it entry or restrict its movement until the risk is addressed.
The Port of Virginia conducts monthly employee training and holds drills with the Coast Guard. Port spokesperson Joe Harris said it had yet to suffer a successful breach.
"We're an economic pinch point," Harris said. "Getting taken offline is not an option."

articles.title_orig: Rare mushrooms found at 'nationally important' site in Keighley
articles.title_zh: Rare mushrooms found at 'nationally important' site in Keighley
articles.content_orig:
A site in Keighley has been recognised as nationally important for grassland fungi, following the discovery of rare mushroom species.
Blackening waxcap, snowy waxcap and apricot club varieties as well as the internationally vulnerable lilac pinkgill have been discovered at the 140-acre Keighley Habitat Bank on the edge of Ilkley Moor,
Once a sheep-grazed pastureland, the site has become a mix of meadows, fens, scrub, grassland and woodland.
Ecologist Thomas Dodds said up to 90% of waxcap grassland habitats had disappeared across Europe, so the find was especially exciting.
"Waxcaps are quite brightly coloured and very large, so they're very beautiful mushrooms," he explained.
"But there's also a lot of other ones in that assemblage of species - some that look like corals, there's some that look like fingers coming out the ground, really, amazing things, amazing colours, amazing shapes.
"The UK is special because we have a lot of sites and we have a lot of examples of this habitat which are really good quality.
"And that's in part due to having lots of areas of unmanaged land where these mushrooms could colonise and have existed for many, many years."
The Keighley site belongs to Environment Bank, which creates biodiversity net gain sites for developers who are required to offset a percentage of the impact of their building as part of planning regulations.
The site neighbours Jacob's Wood and Holden Beck Local Wildlife Site.
Dodds said the fungi played an important role in restoring and maintaining soil health by recycling nutrients, reducing erosion and storing carbon.

articles.title_orig: What’s behind Iran’s escalation of attacks in the Gulf?
articles.title_zh: What’s behind Iran’s escalation of attacks in the Gulf?
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump told Fox News on Sunday that he was inclined to resume strikes on Iran after the new year, and warned that Iranian ships trying to run the US naval blockade would be sunk.
Asked about reports that Iran planned to test the blockade, Trump said: "I hope they do, they'll all be at the bottom of the sea like the rest of the navy," Fox News correspondent Trey Yingst reported.
Based on his conversation with Trump, there was no sign that Tehran was ready to make a deal, Yingst said. Trump told him he had seen videos of renewed protests in Iran and urged the protesters to keep going.
Iran still has about 1,500 ballistic missiles and can produce about 50 a month, the Wall Street Journal has reported.
Two US aircraft carrier strike groups are operating in the Arabian Sea, and US refueling aircraft are based in Israel, Yingst said. Persian Gulf states, which bore the brunt of Iranian fire during the war, have been urging a negotiated settlement, with Qatar passing messages between Washington and Tehran.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that diplomatic efforts were continuing despite heightened tensions with the United States, according to Iranian media.
Araghchi provided an update on the latest diplomatic developments, emphasizing that "the path of diplomacy continues."
Iranian economist and researcher Mohammad Maljou said he had been sentenced to one year in prison based on his writings and academic activities, adding that he was prevented from speaking at either of his two court hearings.
Maljou said Sunday that interrogators from the Revolutionary Guards' intelligence organization prepared the report used to justify his conviction. The precise criminal charge underlying the sentence has yet to be established.
In November 2025, IRGC intelligence agents searched Maljou's home, confiscated electronic devices and books, and subjected him to three lengthy interrogations. He subsequently announced that he would respond only to judicial authorities.
Seven oil tankers have been struck in the Strait of Hormuz since November 16, including three vessels hit by unidentified projectiles near Oman's coast in a 15-hour period, the Joint Maritime Information Centre said. In its Sunday advisory, distributed by UK Maritime Trade Operations, JMIC said the three latest attacks occurred on November 20 and 21, targeting outbound tankers between 8 and 17 nautical miles from Khasab, Oman. Two of the vessels were struck about 50 minutes apart.
The center reported continued Revolutionary Guards activity involving drone overflights, surveillance of commercial ships and occasional radio warnings. It said Iranian claims that tankers had struck naval mines remained unconfirmed by official authorities. Commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remained severely restricted. According to the report, tracking data showed no recorded transits by cargo-carrying vessels above 1,000 deadweight tons between November 19 and 21.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations said Sunday it had received a report of an incident involving an oil tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman.
The maritime security agency said authorities were aware of the incident and investigations were underway. It advised vessels in the area to remain vigilant and monitor the evolving security situation.
UKMTO provided no further details about the incident, including the identity of the tanker or the military forces involved.
Iran should build a nuclear bomb once and for all to strengthen its military deterrence against the United States and Israel, a senior Iranian lawmaker said Sunday, calling for a fundamental change in Tehran's nuclear doctrine.
Ahmad Bakhshayesh Ardestani, a member of parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, told the Iranian news outlet Tabnak that US and Israeli attacks had strengthened arguments for developing nuclear weapons, despite warnings from China and Russia against such a move.
"Therefore, it would be better to build and possess a nuclear bomb once and for all to benefit from its deterrence, even if we never use it," he said.
Bakhshayesh Ardestani also said Iran was sending three supertankers to China, warning that a US attack on even one of the tankers would intensify direct military confrontation, adding that Tehran had threatened to strike oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Kuwait if its vessels were targeted.
The lawmaker said Iran had overcome weaknesses in its air defenses and air force, improved its radar and surveillance capabilities, and extended its missile range from 2,000 to 4,500 kilometers, bringing US military bases in Europe within reach.
He also argued that Washington could not sustain its costly naval blockade indefinitely, describing the Strait of Hormuz as a powerful strategic weapon and proposing fees or restrictions on ships from countries imposing sanctions on Iran.
Two oil tankers caught fire Sunday after striking naval mines in restricted waters east of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's navy said in a statement.
The navy said the vessels entered the restricted area despite previous warnings, with their identification and navigation systems switched off.
It warned that shipowners and operators who disregard maritime restrictions would bear responsibility for any resulting damage. The identities of the tankers and the extent of the damage remain unclear.
Religious rulings can change over time, with Islamic clerics potentially reaching different conclusions on the same issue, a senior Iranian Revolutionary Guards commander said Sunday.
Mohammad Jafar Asadi, former deputy commander of the IRGC's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, was answering a question about the religious permissibility of building atomic bombs when he told Iranian media that such rulings depended on the views of qualified Islamic jurists, known as mujtahids .
"Religious rulings can change," Asadi said. "One jurist may say it is obligatory, while another may say it is recommended or discouraged."
His remarks highlight the flexibility of religious interpretations under Shiite jurisprudence and raise questions about the durability of the nuclear weapons ban attributed to the late Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Tehran has long cited Khamenei's religious decree, or fatwa , prohibiting nuclear weapons as evidence of its commitment to a peaceful nuclear program.
The comments come amid growing debate in Iran over changing its nuclear doctrine following US and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Saturday that supporters of developing nuclear weapons had their arguments, but emphasized that Iran's official nuclear policy remained unchanged.
he Arab League condemned Iran's attack on a civilian industrial facility in Bahrain on Sunday, calling it a violation of Bahrain's sovereignty and of international law.
The attack threatened Bahrain's security, stability and territorial integrity and risked escalating tensions in the region, the League said in a statement. It expressed full solidarity with Bahrain's government and people and backed the measures it takes to protect its security.
The League called on the international community to condemn the attack and work to halt further escalation.
Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE condemned the attack earlier on Sunday. Two people were injured in Iranian attacks on Bahrain on Saturday, one of them critically, the Bahraini Interior Ministry said.
Iran must leave the damaging state of “neither war nor peace” with dignity and strength, President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Sunday.
He said resolving the uncertainty could help address many of the country’s problems.
Pezeshkian also said Iran’s adversaries wanted to disrupt production, cause unemployment and fuel public discontent.
He urged Iranians to change their consumption patterns, saying this would frustrate the country’s adversaries.

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”

articles.title_zh: The Stock Market Is Doing Something for Only the 5th Time This Century, and History Says It's Obvious What Comes Next for Stocks
articles.content_orig:
A Rohingya refugee waves Myanmar's national flag as he waits for the arrival of U.N. General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman at a refugee camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 20, 2026.
The world’s top international court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority, more than a million of whom remain displaced.
The verdict , issued Thursday, is the first time a state has been found responsible for committing genocide in the history of the International Court of Justice, which was established in 1945. In a weekslong military campaign in 2017, Myanmar forces killed at least 10,000 people, including up to 2,109 children under five, and forced more than 700,000 others to flee the country’s northern Rakhine State.
The landmark decision could have significant implications for the legal treatment of cases brought under the 1948 Genocide Convention, Melanie O’Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia Law School, tells TIME. That includes South Africa’s pending case alleging that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza , where Israeli forces have killed tens of thousands of people over the past three years.
A spokesperson for Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing told reporters on Friday that the ruling is “unfair.” Min Aung Hlaing was the military’s commander in chief during the 2017 operation.
“It was not a decision made unanimously,” spokesperson Khine Khine Soe said, pointing out that six of the 15 judges dissented. She did not say whether Myanmar would comply with the ruling.
Myanmar’s military junta-backed government denied committing genocide during the proceedings.
Read More: Myanmar’s Dictator Wants to Rebuild Ties With the West
The National Unity Government, a parallel government formed after Myanmar’s 2021 military coup, said on Thursday that it respects the judgment.
For the Rohingya, the ruling is “public acknowledgment in a court of law and in the top court in the world that what happened to them was genocide,” says O’Brien, who has published multiple books on genocide and international criminal law, is working on a book about the Genocide Convention in the ICJ.
Members of the Rohingya community also said the ruling is a historic recognition of the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group.
“Myanmar denies the existence of the Rohingya,” Sayed Ullah, a community leader at a refugee camp in Bangladesh, told the Associated Press , “but now the court made it clear.”
The court’s finding of genocide by a state is a historic first. Two previous genocide cases brought before the ICJ have gone to the merit stages, both arising from the wars that followed the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s.
In 2007, the court ruled on a case brought by Bosnia against Serbia. The court determined that the killing of thousands of Bosniak men and boys in Srebrenica in 1995 was genocide, but it found insufficient evidence to attribute the killings by Bosnian Serb forces to Serbia. Still, the court ruled that Serbia violated its obligation under the Genocide Convention by failing to use its influence over those forces to prevent genocide.
In the second case, which was brought by Croatia against Serbia, the court made no finding that genocide was committed. It instead ruled in a 2015 judgment that Yugoslav army and Serb forces had an intent to ethnically cleanse Croats from Serb-held areas of Croatia, forcing between 80,000 and 100,000 Croats and other non-Serbs to flee the Krajina region between April 1991 and April 1992.
“The Court has not rewritten or expanded the legal definition of genocide” since the earlier cases, Marko Milanovic, a professor of public international law at the University of Reading, said in a statement . “What it has done is take a more flexible approach to the evidence used to establish genocide, particularly the notoriously difficult question of proving genocidal intent.”
The dissenting judges argued that the evidence could support the intent of forced expulsion or collective punishment instead of an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group.
The court ordered Myanmar’s military-backed government to ensure the safe, voluntary return of the Rohingya to the country and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide.
Myanmar has two years to report to the ICJ on its orders of restitution. If it is unable to carry out restitution, the court ordered the government to pay reparations to the Rohingya, the amount of which will be determined at a later stage.
It’s uncertain whether Myanmar will implement the ruling, which is legally binding.
“Therein lies the rub in that there isn’t necessarily a mechanism for enforcing them,” says O’Brien. If Myanmar does not comply, The Gambia, which brought the case to the ICJ, can turn to the United Nations Security Council, which has discretion over whether to act, although China, which has veto power as a member of the council, is friendly to the Myanmar government.
Third party states can also exert pressure on Myanmar to comply with the ruling, such as through direct diplomatic pressure or sanctions on individuals or companies linked to the genocide. On Thursday, the U.K. ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defense attaché and called for an urgent U.N. Security Council meeting to discuss the judgment. ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights (APHR), an independent group of current and former Southeast Asian parliamentarians, called on the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to support implementation of the ruling. Cheah Wui Ling, an associate professor at the National University of Singapore’s faculty of law, says ASEAN is obligated to “act in ways that respect and not undermine” the ruling, given the organization’s commitment to international law.
Cheah says the ruling could give “fresh momentum” to efforts seeking to hold individuals criminally accountable for the genocide, including an investigation in Argentina and a criminal complaint in Indonesia .
The prosecutor at the International Criminal Court also requested an arrest warrant in 2024 for Min Aung Hlaing. The ruling could have a “snowball effect” on that investigation, says Vincent-Joël Proulx, an associate professor at National University of Singapore’s faculty of law and a former special adviser to the ICJ’s president.
Even so, other challenges remain to seeing restitution through, O’Brien says.
Nine years after the mass displacement, more than a million Rohingya refugees live in Bangladesh, with most in camps in Cox’s Bazar. Some refugees told the AP that they want to return home to Myanmar.
Read More: ‘There Is No Hope’: Death and Desperation Take Over the World’s Largest Refugee Camp
Rohingya refugees visit a market at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 17, 2026. Salahuddin Ahmed—AFP/Getty Images
But many of those homes and villages were completely destroyed, O’Brien says. “They have nothing physically to come back to.” She adds that the Rohingya have faced “decades of discrimination and persecution,” and it’s “very difficult to suddenly turn around a culture of hostility and discrimination.”
Restitution is “trying to put the victims in the position that they were in before this had happened,” says O’Brien. But “so many of them have lost family members, and so many of them have been subject to horrific violence and abuse, so they can’t be put in exactly the same position.”
Eyes are now on South Africa’s genocide case against Israel. The case is in a second round of written pleadings and is expected to take at least three more years.
Myanmar’s defense argued that its military operations targeted militants, not civilians. But the court considered a broader “pattern of conduct” by Myanmar, including hate speech, discriminatory laws, displacement, destruction of property, and widespread sexual violence.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk's SpaceX is betting $74 billion on AI data centers. Texas and Arizona want to know who pays for the power
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk's SpaceX is betting $74 billion on AI data centers. Texas and Arizona want to know who pays for the power
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX wants to build a data center in the Arizona desert that would draw 6,000 megawatts of power at full build-out. That is nearly two-thirds of the all-time peak demand that Arizona Public Service, which serves about 1.5 million homes and businesses, hit across its entire system this summer, according to KJZZ .
The Cochise County campus is the larger half of a plan SpaceX announced on Nov. 12 to spend more than $74 billion on two AI supercomputing sites: roughly $50 billion in southeastern Arizona and more than $24 billion at Starbase, Texas, Reuters reported . The company is pitching both as projects that pay for themselves, with on-site power in Texas, dry cooling in Arizona, and promises of lower bills and taxes for neighbors.
Residents, local officials, and now Arizona’s attorney general want proof first. Who covers the cost of the power plants, water, and grid upgrades behind AI, the company or the people who live next door, is quickly becoming the question that decides whether these campuses get built.
The stakes for SpaceX are large. Its AI segment produced more than half of its third-quarter revenue, ahead of rockets and Starlink, according to Reuters, and Fortune has reported on how renting out computing capacity to Anthropic and Google has become central to the company’s valuation. The political ground is shifting under the industry, too: voters sided against data center development in 37 of 38 local ballot contests with complete counts this month, as Fortune reported after the midterms .
The Texas campus is a gas-fired power plant and “super-compute facility” on 444.45 acres near the Port of Brownsville, The Texas Tribune reported . Brownsville de-annexed the land earlier this year at SpaceX’s request, after the company offered $220 million for city water and wastewater projects. The neighboring city of Starbase, which incorporated around SpaceX’s launch site in 2025, then annexed it.
That sequence leaves the project outside the reach of Brownsville’s 90-day data center moratorium, which took effect in early November. The city says its decision was based on the “information and circumstances presented at the time.”
Because the plant would generate its own electricity, SpaceX says the facility won’t draw from the public grid. It will still burn a lot of gas. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality issued an air permit on Nov. 16 that allows 35 natural gas turbines producing 750 megawatts and up to 248 tons of nitrogen oxides a year, Newsweek reported , citing Politico .
The South Texas Environmental Justice Network has announced a protest, arguing the facilities would pollute the air, use up water, and raise residents’ energy bills. Other residents see opportunity. “There’s a lot of people that need jobs in our community and SpaceX has contributed to those jobs,” Janie Melendez, a Brownsville school teacher who previously served on the Texas Republican Party’s executive committee, told the Tribune .
Melendez has felt SpaceX’s pull in another way. “Since SpaceX moved in, my home has tripled in value,” she said. Rising values are a win for owners, but they tend to lift property tax bills and rents, which can squeeze newer residents and renters.
The tax question is now live. On Nov. 17, Cameron County commissioners voted 3-2 against moving ahead with talks on a 10-year, 100% property tax abatement for the project. Starbase’s own city commission is scheduled to consider a tax abatement on Dec. 9. And in January, SpaceX will face a new governor, Gina Hinojosa, who has vowed to freeze data center approvals until lawmakers pass new protections.
The Arizona campus would sit on 747 acres near the Willcox Playa, about 80 miles east of Tucson, according to the Arizona Daily Star . It would take power from the grid through the Sulphur Springs Valley Electric Cooperative and the Arizona Electric Power Cooperative, and SpaceX says the nearby Apache Generating Station, which burns coal and natural gas, would grow from about 1 gigawatt to more than 6 gigawatts. The permit application lists $3.6 billion in planned grid upgrades.
SpaceX’s pitch to the county is aggressive. At a community meeting, Riley Trettle, who heads SpaceX’s energy and supercomputer department, said the project would reduce residents’ electricity bills, lower property taxes by 20%, and create about 1,000 permanent jobs, according to the Star . The application projects a one-time $250 million sales tax benefit for the county and $35 million to $103 million in sales tax revenue, and the company expects about 5,500 construction jobs.
Water is the sharper worry. The campus would be dry-cooled and would not pump groundwater for industrial use, though an existing well could supply up to 10 acre-feet a year for drinking water and maintenance. Residents point to an aquifer already drawn down by large dairy farms, and experts told the Star that the water used to generate the campus’s power could raise annual data center water use by 60% to 90%. The permit doesn’t estimate that figure.
On Nov. 19, Attorney General Kris Mayes asked the Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission to postpone its Dec. 9 vote until state and federal agencies can review the project. Her letter questions how SpaceX would cover power needs beyond what the regional cooperative can generate, and raises concerns about water, fire safety, traffic, wildlife, and nearby Fort Huachuca. “The people of Cochise County deserve answers before county officials approve a project of this magnitude,” Mayes said in a statement . She plans her own town hall at Cochise Elementary School on Dec. 3.
Arizona’s larger utilities are already wrestling with the same cost split. APS describes its approach as “growth pays for growth”: large customers sign long-term contracts so they, rather than residential and small commercial customers, cover the infrastructure they require, Scripps News reported . Data centers accounted for about 7% of APS’s peak load this year, up from about 5% last year, according to KJZZ .
Regulators draw a finer line. Arizona Corporation Commissioner Kevin Thompson says data centers will pay for any new generation they require, but all customers should share reliability investments that benefit the whole grid. “If it’s for the betterment of the grid as a whole, then that peanut butter should be spread across the bread, right?” he told KJZZ.
Meanwhile, APS is asking the commission to approve a 14% to 16% rate increase for residential customers. In that case, an APS witness, Jamie Moe, acknowledged that residential demand isn’t causing high growth-related costs, KJZZ reported.
SpaceX’s Arizona campus would be served by cooperatives rather than APS, but any rate increase would still need the Corporation Commission’s approval. The Dec. 9 votes in Starbase and Cochise County will be the first public tests of whether SpaceX’s promise that its AI campuses will pay their own way holds up once the bills, and the gigawatts, come due.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Stocks Extend Plunge as AI Boom Turns to Bust
articles.title_zh: U.S. Stocks Extend Plunge as AI Boom Turns to Bust
articles.content_orig:
A punishing sell-off in technology stocks intensified Friday, wiping out the Nasdaq Composite’s gains for the year, as investors continued to pull money out of the once high-flying AI trade.
The S&P 500 fell 3.7% and posted its seventh consecutive day of losses — its longest losing streak since February 2020, when Wall Street started bracing for what became the Covid pandemic.
The tech-focused Nasdaq faced even steeper losses on Friday, dropping 5.28%. It is now down more than 2% for the year.
The Nasdaq hit a record high on October 6, and was up as much as 18.7% on the year. Since that all-time high, the index has slumped, erasing all those gains and shedding roughly $8.7 trillion in market value.
“It’s a meltdown right now,” Arun Sundaram, senior vice president of investment strategy at CFRA Research, told CNN in an email. “So much bearish sentiment around tech and AI.”
Even Anthropic’s blockbuster stock market debut quickly lost its shine Friday, with shares in the AI lab dropping 8.5%. They closed at $88.91, just above the company’s IPO of $83.
Why Anthropic’s blockbuster debut didn’t ease Wall Street’s AI fears
The Dow fell 950 points, or 1.93%, posting its fifth consecutive day of losses of more than 1%. The Dow dropped 8% this week, its worst week since March 2020.
The Dow and the S&P 500 closed in correction on Friday, trading down more than 10% from their respective peaks on August 5 and October 6. They join the Nasdaq, which closed in correction earlier this month and is now down 18% since its record high on October 6.
Meanwhile, the Nasdaq and S&P 500 suffered their worst week since early April 2025, when President Donald Trump’s tariff plans rocked global markets.
Stocks associated with the AI trade have been in a serious rough patch for weeks now. But with Anthropic’s buzzy IPO now in the rear-view mirror, traders’ concerns about the broader industry are once again coming to the fore.
It’s the year of the mega AI IPO. Should you invest?
“There is a real exodus out of tech stocks,” Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at the online brokerage platform Interactive Brokers, told CNN. “Buy the dip has been taking a back seat to sell the rally – or just sell.”
“The tech sector is just getting walloped,” Sosnick said.
Investors are grappling with a bevy of concerns, from uncertainty over how newly elected Democratic governors will impact the pace of the data center buildout to uncertainty about the future of Nvidia’s role in powering the AI industry’s growth after CEO Jensen Huang resigned.
“There is a fear that maybe there is too much froth and enthusiasm in the tech bet given all the risks out there,” said David Kelly, chief global strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management.
Kelly noted that corrections are “inevitable” and there is “nothing particularly ominous” about a correction given how much US stocks have rallied in recent years.
“This is not a fatal illness. It’s not even the flu. At the moment, it looks like a mild cold, and it should be over in a week or two,” he said.
Another growing concern for investors: Companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on the AI buildout, using their own cash and also tapping the debt and equity markets to raise more capital.
For awhile, investors cheered the AI spending. But now, they’re getting more serious about demanding evidence of return on investment.
“The market was already questioning some of the cost-benefit analysis … and you’re coming off of relatively euphoric levels. Put all that together, that’s a lot for the market to bear,” Sosnick at Interactive Brokers told CNN.
In a sign of growing nervousness among investors, the VIX, which tracks expectations for volatility and is known as Wall Street’s ‘fear gauge,’ surged 86% this week and closed at 35.89 on Friday — its highest level in 19 months. Generally, a level above 20 indicates heightened investor uncertainty.
The sell-off sent investors looking for safer corners of the market, like US Treasury bonds, which rallied sharply on Friday.
Corners of the AI trade that have been in the spotlight in recent weeks were among the names under pressure. CoreWeave, the neocloud backed by Nvidia, slumped 12% Friday. CoreWeave’s IPO price in March 2025 was $40 a share — it’s trading at $39.51 now, wiping out all gains since it debuted on the market.
Trump defends Putin relationship and says he’ll stop US companies from building data centers abroad
Nvidia dropped 14% on Friday, its worst day in almost two years. The chip giant tumbled 22.9% on the week, posting its worst week since October 2008.
Reuters reported Friday that the US Securities and Exchange Commission is probing Nvidia over its accounting practices, adding to pressure on the stock.
Nvidia has plunged 47.5% since its October 6 peak, shedding $2.7 trillion in market value. That’s larger than the individual market value of every company in the S&P 500 except Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet and Nvidia itself.
The sell-off has been so severe that tech stocks may suddenly look cheap to some investors. US tech stock valuations, as measured by the forward price-to-earnings ratio of the S&P 500’s info tech sector, entered Friday at their lowest level since March 2020, according to FactSet.
As for Nvidia? The forward P/E ratio for the next 12 months is the lowest since 2002.
That has some strategists suggesting that widespread fears might be overblown.
“I don’t fully understand it, as the fundamentals don’t really justify all this selling,” said Sundaram from CFRA Research. “But right now, it’s sell now and worry about the fundamentals later.”

articles.title_orig: Ranked: The Vehicles Most Likely to Last 250,000 Miles
articles.title_zh: Ranked: The Vehicles Most Likely to Last 250,000 Miles
articles.content_orig:
For many car buyers, reliability is about more than avoiding repairs. It’s also about how long a vehicle can remain on the road before it needs to be replaced.
Reaching 250,000 miles (approximately 400,000 km) is a major milestone for drivers hoping to get the most value from their purchase.
This infographic ranks the vehicles with the highest estimated probability of reaching that milestone. The data comes from iSeeCars’ Longest Lasting Cars Study , published in September 2026.
Based on mileage data from more than 395 million vehicles, the study estimates each model’s likelihood of reaching 250,000 miles. It excludes heavy-duty vehicles, models with insufficient data, and vehicles discontinued by 2022.
Toyota’s presence is the clearest pattern in the data, with 10 models making the top 27.
Add five Lexus models, and the two brands account for 15 entries, or approximately 56% of the ranking.
The Lexus LS ranks second at 38.8%, followed by the Toyota 4Runner at 33.1%. Together with the Sequoia, these models give Toyota and Lexus all three top positions.
Toyota’s reputation for reliability is closely linked to its focus on quality control and continuous improvement.
The company’s Toyota Production System emphasizes identifying manufacturing defects early, allowing workers to stop production and address problems before vehicles leave the factory.
Toyota also says it applies rigorous quality standards across vehicle development, manufacturing, and its supplier network.
Larger vehicles feature prominently near the top, including the Toyota Sequoia, 4Runner, Tundra, and Tacoma.
The Tundra has a 28.2% estimated chance of reaching 250,000 miles, while the Tacoma comes in at 25.0%.
However, longevity is not limited to trucks and SUVs. The Toyota Avalon ranks eighth at 23.2%, while the Honda Civic makes the list at 15.0%, showing that smaller passenger cars can also perform well.
For buyers considering long-term ownership costs, durability is only part of the equation. Another important factor is depreciation, as shown in our ranking of the cars that hold and lose their value the most.
Six hybrid models appear in the ranking, led by the Lexus RX Hybrid at 28.9% and Toyota Highlander Hybrid at 20.7%.
The Honda Accord Hybrid follows at 18.5%, while the Toyota Avalon Hybrid, Prius, and Camry Hybrid also make the list.
More broadly, Toyota, Lexus, Honda, and Acura collectively account for 25 of the 27 ranked vehicles. The only exceptions are the Mercedes-Benz G-Class at 17.3% and Chevrolet Suburban at 11.6%, highlighting how heavily this ranking favors Japanese automakers.

Ram and GMC average more than several luxury brands, while eight major car brands still come in below $40,000.
The average new vehicle in America cost a record $51,109 in October 2026. But what buyers pay varies dramatically by brand, reflecting differences in vehicle size, model selection, and the types of cars Americans choose.
This graphic ranks average U.S. new-vehicle transaction prices across 31 brands, using Kelley Blue Book data from Cox Automotive . Figures reflect prices before consumer incentives, taxes, and fees, and the industry average includes brands outside this ranking.
Ram averaged $69,850 in October, while GMC averaged $65,607. Both ranked ahead of luxury brands including Audi ($64,403), Genesis ($64,316), Lexus ($63,899), and Volvo ($61,588).
Vehicle mix helps explain the gap. Ram’s lineup centers on pickups and vans, and full-size pickups averaged $67,912 across the U.S. market in October, while full-size SUVs reached $80,957.
The table below ranks all 31 brands by their October 2026 average transaction prices and year-over-year percentage changes:
Average prices span nearly $92,000 across the ranking.
Porsche led second-place Land Rover ($102,826) by more than $22,000, while Chevrolet ($51,058) landed just $51 below the industry average.
European automakers occupy four of the six most expensive positions, led by Porsche ($125,270) and Land Rover ($102,826). BMW ($73,149) and Mercedes-Benz ($71,086) also rank among the top six.
This reflects the luxury-heavy mix of European brands in the U.S. market. Six of the eight European brands listed average more than $61,000, with MINI ($41,075) and Volkswagen ($40,185) as the exceptions.
These higher averages largely reflect the types of vehicles European brands sell in America, rather than a direct price comparison between equivalent models.
Japanese and South Korean brands account for seven of the eight automakers averaging below $40,000. Toyota sits just above that group at $44,168, nearly $7,000 below the industry average.
Many Asian automakers sell their upscale vehicles under separate badges, including Lexus, Acura, Genesis, and Infiniti. Their mainstream brands continue to offer smaller cars and crossovers, helping keep average transaction prices lower.
For context, compact cars averaged $28,030 in October, compared with $37,895 for compact SUVs. Demand for more affordable vehicles also remains strong, with Kelley Blue Book reporting a 9.6% year-over-year increase in sales of vehicles priced around $28,000 to $38,000.
Buick is the only American brand averaging below $40,000, at $37,400. Although its lineup consists entirely of SUVs, it lacks the full-size pickups that lift averages at Ford, Chevrolet, and GMC.
Overall, the ranking highlights how vehicle mix, rather than brand prestige alone, shapes what Americans pay for new cars.

Compare monthly fuel costs for America’s best-selling cars, from $43 electric Teslas to a $245 diesel Silverado over 900 miles.
A vehicle’s sticker price is only part of what drivers pay over time. Fuel efficiency and powertrain choice can make a significant difference in ongoing expenses, even between versions of the same model.
This visualization compares the estimated monthly fuel and electricity costs of 30 versions of popular U.S. vehicles, including pickup trucks, SUVs, sedans, and electric cars.
The figures come from Kadoa , using underlying information from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, U.S. Energy Information Administration, and Cox Automotive.
The calculations assume 900 miles of driving per month, using U.S. gasoline prices as of October 19, 2026, and electricity rates from August 2026. Electric vehicle costs assume home charging.
Diesel-powered pickup trucks top the ranking, with the Chevrolet Silverado having the highest estimated monthly fuel cost at $245, followed closely by the GMC Sierra at $240. The gasoline-powered Ford F-Series ranks third at $203 per month.
Larger pickup trucks tend to have higher fuel costs because of their weight, size, and fuel consumption. The estimates also highlight differences between powertrains, with the hybrid Ford F-Series costing $39 less per month than its gasoline counterpart.
Comparing gasoline and hybrid versions of the same model reveals some of the clearest savings. The Ford Maverick’s estimated monthly fuel cost falls from $157 for gasoline to $104 for the hybrid, a difference of $53 per month or $636 a year.
The hybrid Kia Sportage costs $101 per month versus $148 for its gasoline counterpart, while the Honda Civic hybrid comes in at $79 versus $113.
While hybrid versions generally carry a higher upfront purchase price, their improved fuel efficiency can help offset that premium over time, particularly for drivers covering more miles.

articles.title_orig: From Anthropic to Nvidia, Wall Street just had a bizarre, wild week
articles.title_zh: From Anthropic to Nvidia, Wall Street just had a bizarre, wild week
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic’s share price slump triggered a sharp sell-off on Wall Street with tech stocks closing down more than 5pc.
More than $163bn was wiped off the value of the AI giant on Friday, just a day after it touched a $2tn valuation on its stock market debut.
The decline prompted a wider flight from AI shares, with the tech-focused Nasdaq 100 down 5.6pc. It means the index has now erased all its gains year to date.
The S&P 500 fell 3.7pc at close, putting it on course for its worst week since Donald Trump’s ‘liberation day’ tariffs last year, and into correction territory.
Anthropic has endured a hugely volatile introduction to public markets, surging as much as 39pc on the Nasdaq on Thursday, before closing the day 17pc higher.
However, it fell by as much as 14pc to $83.16 on Friday, just above where it started trading on Thursday.
It started the day at $97, less than 24 hours after it hit a high of $115.
The latest sell-off has fuelled fears that the company’s record-breaking float, which raised $87bn, is not enough to dispel lingering concerns over the AI bubble.
It comes after a series of threats to the investment boom.
That includes anti-data centre Democrats taking control of Congress, the downfall of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and tighter export controls on chips to China.
The Philadelphia semiconductor index, a grouping of the major US chip companies, dropped by as much as 9pc on Friday.
AI-linked companies dragged the Nasdaq lower, with the likes of semiconductor maker ARM losing 14pc.
CoreWeave also weighed on the Nasdaq, with its shares down 12pc.
European shares were also on track for their worst week since March amid investor concern over an AI bubble.
In a day of volatile swings on Wall Street, Nvidia also slipped behind Google parent Alphabet to become the fourth-most valuable US company.
Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “It’s been another hectic and negative week and one where even positive news is struggling to help the market stabilise.”
Pressure on stocks also rose after Donald Trump on Friday threatened to ban technology companies from building data centres outside of the US.
In a White House press conference, Mr Trump warned there would be “tremendous penalties” on US companies that tried to build data centres in foreign countries.
He said: “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen.”
He added: “We’re going to fight very hard for the data centres because we’re not going to let China [overtake us].”
The ban threat will raise questions for AI developers who are spending hundreds of billions of pounds building data facilities in the UK, Europe and across Asia.
It is not clear whether Mr Trump’s ban would apply to all data centre developers or just the most advanced facilities.
The sell-off came as Anthropic’s approach to copyright was slammed by news publishers, who said the company lacks “a basic moral compass”.
The News Media Association (NMA), which represents titles including The Telegraph, The Times and The Guardian, attacked the company for its policy on journalism.
Anthropic told investors it could not guarantee it would adhere to measures that prevented journalism from being used to train AI models.
The Claude maker said it took steps to abide by paywalls but that this “may not always be successful”.
Thank you for following our live coverage of the tech sell-off in the US.
Keep up to date with the latest business news here.
The Nasdaq 100 has extended its decline to 5.6pc lower after a bruising day for the tech sector, with the S&P 500 also dropping further to close 3.7pc down.
Anthropic shares meanwhile closed down 8.5pc, currently trading at $89.
The Dow Jones has also continued its fall, down 1.9pc for the day.
Nvidia shares are now down 13.7pc.
The Philadelphia semiconductor index, a grouping of the major US chip companies, dropped by 10.7pc on Friday.
Apple, which is seen as less exposed to the AI industry, saw its shares fall 1.8pc.
Microsoft shares fell 2.8pc.
Treasury yields have fallen after a widespread tech sell-off prompted investors to seek out safe havens for their cash.
The move, which reduces US borrowing costs, saw 2-year treasury yields fall 0.16pc, with the yield on 10-year notes also falling.
Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital, believes markets are now entering a more defensive phase.
“Strong AI demand and successful individual listings are no longer sufficient to sustain broader risk appetite when investors are questioning valuations, borrowing costs and the outlook for corporate profitability.”
Lawrence Gillum, of LPL Financial, noted: “This is your classic flight-to-safety trade. So as investors are getting a little bit ​more concerned about the AI trade, they’re moving out of those stocks and into Treasury securities.
“Anytime there’s been some sort of hiccup in the AI trade, we’ve seen ​the Treasury market rally on the back of that.”
The Nasdaq 100 has extended its decline to 4.5pc lower since the opening bell, with the S&P 500 also dropping further to 2.8pc.
Anthropic shares meanwhile have stabilised somewhat, currently trading at $87.
The Dow Jones has also continued its fall into correction territory, down 1pc for the day.
Nvidia shares are now down 11.4pc.
Nvidia shares have now fallen 9.2pc, extending losses for a session which has seen the chipmaker slip behind Alphabet to become the fourth-most ‌valuable US company.
The stock remains on course ​for its seventh straight weekly decline, its longest losing streak since 2008.
The tech giant has been unable to shake anxieties over its leadership following the abrupt departure of co-founder Jensen ​Huang.
Nvidia and Anthropic, who have massive compute infrastructure deals together, both suffered heavy drops on Friday.
Anthropic shares are slowly rising from their low of $83, matching the price issued at the start of their IPO on Thursday.
The AI frontier developer’s stock is now worth $86 per share, but remains 11pc down for the session.
The Nasdaq Composite, which Anthropic now lists in, remains 3.6pc down.
Chipmakers have suffered a major sell-off on Friday as investors retreat from AI-linked stocks.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks the major US chip firms, tumbled 8.4pc, weighted down by the likes of AMD and Broadcom, down 10.5pc and 11pc respectively.
Nvidia, the world largest chipmaker, is down 7.1pc.
Donald Trump has threatened to ban technology companies from building data centres outside of the US, raising fresh doubts over dozens of projects being developed by AI giants around the world.
In a White House press conference, Mr Trump warned there would be “tremendous penalties” on US companies that tried to build data centres in foreign countries.
He said: “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen.”
He added: “We’re going to fight very hard for the data centres because we’re not going to let China [overtake us].”
The ban threat will raise questions for AI developers who are spending hundreds of billions of pounds building data facilities in the UK, Europe and across Asia.
Some of these are for building cutting-edge AI bots. Others are for keeping them running queries or for keeping the internet operating smoothly. It is not clear whether Mr Trump’s ban would apply to all data centre developers or just the most advanced facilities.
The Nasdaq 100 has fallen to 4pc lower since Mr Trump’s comments.
